subtopic: PROVISION OF AIR TRANSPORTATION AND MAINTENANCE PERSONNEL

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: PROVISION OF AIR TRANSPORTATION AND MAINTENANCE PERSONNEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a result of the recent outbreaks of violence in the Congo a serious shortage of internal air transportation and maintenance personnel has developed. This matter was brought to the attention of the various countries concerned by the United Nations secretariat at a special meeting on September 20, when a general request was made for any assistance possible. This request was further amplified on September 22, when more details were furnished as to the exact requirements.
On September 23 the government agreed to provide assistance, and appropriate orders were issued. Two C-119 aircraft of 436 squadron, R.C.A.F., Downsview, left their base at 9.14 and 10.44 on the morning of Sunday, September 24. A C-130B and North Star were also despatched to carry the personnel and extra stores, spare parts, etc., required. These two latter aircraft will return from the Congo immediately they have delivered their cargoes.
Over and above the C-119 detachment, 12 highly qualified supervisory technicians have been provided to assist the United Nations Congo maintenance organization. The entire detachment and supervisors, totalling approximately 80 all ranks, should be in position in the Congo by 7.40 Congo time, Tuesday evening, September 26.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-131, to encourage fitness and amateur sport.
He said: Mr. Speaker, as was evident in the debate on the resolution, all parties have welcomed the initiative being taken through this bill. As President Kennedy has said of his country:
The physical fitness of our citizens is a vital prerequisite to America's realization of its full potential as a nation, and to the opportunities of each individual citizen to make full and fruitful use of his capacities.

No one, I am sure, will dispute that these words apply with equal force to Canada, or that the legislation now being introduced fills a long felt need.
In presenting these new proposals for the encouragement of fitness and amateur sport we are fully conscious of the fact that we are dealing with a complex and dynamic aspect of Canadian life on which there are widely varying views. Anyone familiar with this field will be aware of the broad range of activities involved, and of the problems to be faced in endeavouring to work out a sound and practical piece of legislation within which such a program can grow and develop in line with both present and future needs.
Even so, it is our view that the bill now before the house will offer an opportunity to achieve most of the things which have been advocated over the years by lay and professional leaders in the fields of fitness, recreation and amateur sport. But as I pointed out in speaking to the resolution, we would welcome any suggestions which would improve the program as now envisaged. Even in its final form this measure might have its shortcomings, which could become apparent as it comes into operation, and which could require amendments to be made from time to time in order to permit the achievement of its full intent.
Furthermore, we have recognized that the objectives of this program cannot be attained in a vacuum. They can only be reached through the network of recreational programs operated by public agencies as well as by the many non-governmental organizations devoted to fitness and amateur sport. We hope that with the full co-operation of professional leaders and volunteer workers it will be possible to add a new dimension to these activities throughout Canada.
I should like to pay a warm tribute to all those who for many years have been labouring actively in these fields. I hope they will regard this new legislation as the fulfilment of their faith and vision; for our expectation is that building on their efforts, this present initiative will furnish that new spark and that new dynamic leadership necessary to achieve a sound, broadly based and sustained effort all across the country. It is this type of pattern which unfortunately in the past seems to have eluded our grasp.
Hon. members will note that the legislation places considerable emphasis on assistance for amateur sport. We are all aware that in the case of professional sport, revenues are considerable, stemming not only from paid admissions but also from various sources such as television and radio. Amateur sport has, unfortunately, lacked the same degree of support. This has meant inadequate financing

for the whole range of amateur athletics, as well as for programs specifically designed for fitness.
Obviously further financial aid is urgently required if existing services for the development of fitness and amateur sport are to be strengthened and extended. Our new program is aimed at fulfilling this requirement. With the assistance now proposed it is possible to foresee a whole new development with respect to sports events supported by federal and provincial governments. We would hope, too, that federal activities in relation to international and national programs would complement and supplement those of the provinces.
In this connection, we are very anxious to assist with joint projects organized and administered by the provinces on a basis that is acceptable to them. Certainly-and I want to make this abundantly clear-the dominion government will be most careful in respecting the rights of the provinces and of local governments in this field, for we are fully aware that if the program is to succeed it must enjoy the wholehearted support of the provinces and, through them, of municipal authorities as well as of local groups within the communities themselves.
There is one further point I would make in relation to the program's scope. The new undertaking will not be concerned solely with the gifted athlete who may be in a position to take part in national and international competitions. It will also be concerned with fitness and sports programs for the great mass of our population. Here I would stress that even the large sum being made available under this program represents but a small part of the total effort required to develop well balanced recreational activities across Canada.
In perusing this bill the house will naturally be interested in comparing its provisions with those of the national fitness act of 1943. Perhaps one or two comments would be helpful on this point. The most significant difference is the amount of financial support provided in the new legislation. The present act makes available the substantial sum of $5 million annually, or about 22 times the amount allocated for somewhat similar purposes under the former provision. I think there can be little doubt that the relatively small sum and the manner in which it was made available under the previous program tended to hamper the work of the then national physical fitness council.
In the years since the 1943 act was introduced, very considerable changes have taken place in Canada. Our population has increased from less than 12 million to over 18 million people. During the interval, provincial
Advisory Council on Sports and local governments as well as sports groups and organizations have devoted a great deal of effort to the strengthening and extension of fitness and amateur sport programs.
Moreover, the climate of public opinion, as indicated in the many representations received by the dominion government, has changed considerably since the repeal of the former act. As I pointed out in discussing the resolution, there appears to be a growing awareness of the importance of fitness both to the individual and to the nation. Here an important factor has been the advent of new means of communication such as television. The fact that many sports activities are now brought into our homes-whether from another part of Canada or another part of the globe-has done much to stimulate the interest of Canadians in such activities.
Over and above this, Canadian participation in international competitive events is emerging as an important aspect of a growing spirit of nationhood. In the representations made to the government over the past few years, strong desire has been expressed to see government financial aid provided to assist our athletes in competition abroad.
Another distinction between the legislation before us today and the act of 1943 is that the amount of $5 million is set out as a statutory item to be provided each year. No fund is established, as was done under the former act. By making allocations available on a statutory basis the federal commitment will be clearly known, and it will thus be possible for the new advisory council to suggest projects and advise on priorities with the firm expectation that adequate funds will be available from year to year. Continuing commitments and major undertakings requiring a number of years to complete will have as much assurance of financial support as it is possible to give.
At the same time, the statutory approach will provide an important safeguard. Any amounts not expended in a fiscal year will lapse. This means, for example, that in the first few years, when expenditures may be -and I repeat, "may be"-somewhat lower while programs are getting under way, funds will not accumulate in a manner which might lead to a lack of concern for ensuring their careful expenditure.
A fourth important difference in the present legislation as compared with the former act relates to the council. The national physical fitness council established in 1943 was a body with executive authority. Under our new provisions the council will be advisory to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, and expenditures will be subject to the

Advisory Council on Sports usual government scrutiny and control. In following this approach we have, of course, looked to the experience gained through the advisory committee on vocational training, the advisory committee for rehabilitation of disabled persons, and the dominion council of health.
A fifth and final point of difference is the fact that the new program will place considerable emphasis on federal aid for national and international sports events.
To sum up, then, we believe we have now developed a program that is more comprehensive, better rounded, and more in keeping with the needs of the people of Canada than that which was formerly in force. In so doing we have tried to benefit from the mistakes of the past, and to lay the groundwork for an undertaking which will provide greater opportunity for harmonious growth in the future.
Turning to the specific objectives of the bill, the house will note that there is provision of assistance "for the promotion and development of Canadian participation in national and international amateur sport." An important aspect of this objective will be furnishing encouragement and assistance to Canada's more gifted athletes in national and international competitions, this to involve the co-operation of national sports organizations. In the past many Canadian athletes with real potential have not had an opportunity to develop to their fullest extent because of the lack of facilities and qualified coaching. Others have not found it possible to pursue amateur sports beyond local competitions even though they may have had the ability to enter national and international sports events. We would hope that when this program fully develops it will offer greater opportunities for persons with athletic ability to participate to the utmost in athletic pursuits of their choice.
In extending greater assistance to Canadian participation in international sporting events, we are merely doing what many other nations have done over the years, and we hope this will help assure a greater measure of parity for our athletes in relation to their fellow competitors from other countries. In taking this action we are also recognizing the fact that Canadians who compete in the Olympics, the British empire and commonwealth games, the Pan-American games and other international championship competitions are ambassadors of good will for Canada. In this connection it should be noted that support by the dominion government must carry with it a responsibility on the part 

of our athletes. Canada will expect them to exemplify the highest standards of sportsmanship on all occasions.
In developing a formula for federal aid with respect to international competitions, we shall need the advice of the agencies which organize such events, the Canadian Olympic Association, the British empire and commonwealth games association, and the Pan-American games committee. Other sports-governing bodies covering fields not included in these events are also concerned in Canadian participation abroad and these, together with the Canadian sports advisory council, will, I am sure, all have valuable suggestions on how federal support might be provided on an equitable basis. Here again is an area where the advice of the new national council will be of particular importance.
The new program will give major emphasis to promoting amateur sports and fitness for all our young people. Much of the development in this area has centered around community and school athletic programs and so comes within the jurisdiction of provincial and municipal governments. Accordingly we shall be looking to the provinces for suggestions and guidance in this field. Having in mind the valuable experience we have already had in working with provincial authorities under programs such as the national health grants, vocational training and vocational rehabilitation, I have no doubt it will be possible to work out mutually satisfactory arrangements without much difficulty.
In promoting wider participation in amateur sport and recreation, there is a need for more facilities of both the indoor and outdoor variety. Here the federal government plans to move forward in a number of ways to assist with expansion and development.
I might mention, first, that the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources is continuing to give considerable attention to the expansion of recreational facilities in national parks. Second, there is the important federal contribution being made through the municipal winter works program in the construction of recreational facilities across Canada. Through the co-operative effort of the various levels of government, the Department of Labour can approve projects covering the construction of community rinks, community swimming pools and playgrounds, stadia and playing fields, as well as other recreational facilities. In the last fiscal year outlays under this program amounted to some $15 million, of which the federal treasury paid $3,800,000 for parks, playgrounds and other recreational facilities. Thus while the main objective of the winter works program is to provide useful employment for persons out of work, it has also had as an important

by-product the increase in community recreational facilities across Canada. Incidentally, in these projects alone some 11,000 individuals were employed last year.
A further impetus to the development of such facilities will be afforded by the program we are now discussing. Among other things, it is hoped that this new effort will make it possible to develop some fitness and amateur sport facilities at the federal and provincial level through which courses for coaches and other leaders can be provided. In this connection we plan to seek suggestions from the national advisory council.
Speaking of courses for coaches and other leaders, hon. members will note the bill's provisions for the training of personnel. The emphasis on coaches is deliberate, because we are convinced that if we are to assist young Canadians effectively to discover and develop their capabilities, the number of competent coaches must be increased many times. We believe the potential athletic ability of our young people to be second to none in the world, but it is obvious that they have been handicapped by the lack of opportunities to obtain the proper training. While we cannot expect results overnight, there is every reason to believe that over a period, very satisfactory progress can be made.
Another area in which assistance could be given would be in relieving the shortage of suitably trained persons. As outlined in the bill, this objective may be met through the provision of bursaries and fellowships to provide for graduate training for professional personnel needed in fitness and amateur sports activities. I would also emphasize the importance of voluntary personnel. In a people's program such as we hope this will be, the extensive use of voluntary leadership is essential. One of the major problems for consideration, therefore, will be the ways and means by which progress can be furthered in this area.
A further objective of the new program will be the undertaking or assisting in research or surveys in respect to fitness and amateur sport. Here we have endeavoured to make provision for a variety of projects. For example, there has been a recurring demand for the inventory type of survey of recreational services, facilities and personnel. Many provinces may wish to assess their existing services, facilities and their personnel needs as a part of the long term development of their programs. In all likelihood surveys of this type will receive considerable prominence in the early stages of the new program. In such research projects there would also be a place for studies related to the development of standards.
Advisory Council on Sports
Another research area in need of financial aid is fitness. Much remains to be learned of the extent to which fitness depends on the mechanical and functional efficiency of the body. The rapid advances in physiology made possible by recent developments in electronic, biochemical and photographic instruments of research have opened up new avenues of investigation. In March of this year the Canadian Medical Association and the Canadian association for health, physical education and recreation held a joint conference on physical fitness. The research personnel attending this meeting included physiologists, neurologists, biochemists, cardiologists, medical doctors, and physical educators qualified to conduct research. Their discussions indicated many gaps in our present knowledge and pointed to the fact that research should be undertaken on the following general problems:
Collection of precise anthropometric data on Canadian school children of all ages in different provinces and information on the combined effect of growth and exercise on stature, weight, muscular and skeletal development.
Measurement of the physical working capacity of representative sections of the Canadian population, both for accurate comparison with data from other countries and to enable changes over the course of years to be observed and measured.
Study of the effect of continuing physical activity or inactivity on normal biological ageing.
Study of the relationship between physical activity and specific disease morbidity.
Study of effect of different types of activity on physical performance.
From these suggestions it is obvious that there are important areas of research to be developed and assisted. We anticipate that this aspect of the new program will be patterned after procedures used in connection with other federal research grants. A panel of research scientists will be established to consider projects submitted for financial support, and liaison will be maintained with other research programs to ensure a coordination of effort and to avoid overlapping.
On the matter of the provision of awards, the house will recall that the former national physical fitness council granted the national amateur athletic achievement award, and that the first recipient was Miss Barbara Ann Scott. This practice of providing certificates, citations or awards of merit is common in many countries as a means of giving national recognition for outstanding accomplishment.

Advisory Council on Sports We will be looking to the new advisory council for suggestions on the best manner of making such provisions in Canada.
The final objective I would mention is the preparation and distribution of information. Different media may, of course, be used including printed material, films, radio and television. For example, films and film strips may prove helpful in coaching courses. We would also look to an extension of departmental publications on fitness and recreation, which over the years have been very well received and most of which have been made available on a "for sale" basis.
These are some of the directions in which I would expect increased progress to be made through the stimulus of the new legislation. In clause 4 the bill provides for grants to agencies and organizations carrying on activities in the fields of fitness and amateur sport. As I have already mentioned, a satisfactory basis of support will have to be developed to ensure the equitable and effective use of funds. This will not be an easy task but is one which I am sure can be worked out in co-operation with the agencies concerned and with the advice of the new national council.
As to clause 5, considerable discussion with the provinces will obviously be required concerning federal-provincial agreements related to the payment of federal contributions for provincial projects under this program. The basis of distribution of funds among the provinces and matching and non-matching features of grants are but a few of the questions which will be of vital concern here.
The details with respect to both clauses 4 and 5 will be set out in orders in council. This feature we intend to borrow from the national health grants. In this way the formula of assistance and the basis of continuing support can be dealt with in some detail but, at the same time, some flexibility can be afforded in making the changes and adjustments which will arise in developing the program. In the case of assistance to the provinces, of course, any changes affecting the agreements with the dominion government are covered by the provisions of clause 6 of the legislation. This ensures that amendments will be dealt with either through a method of amendment agreed upon and included in the agreement itself or by the mutual consent of the federal and provincial governments.
Clause 7 covers the establishment of a national advisory council on fitness and amateur sport, to which I have already made reference many times in the course of these


remarks. It would, of course, be premature at this stage to discuss its membership in any detail, but it will be noted that at least one member shall be appointed from each province. There will also be representation from the federal government. The remaining membership will be derived from various non-governmental sources. A major problem will be to ensure a balance of interest in the wide range of activities covered by the new legislation. We would hope that this could be achieved with a council of from 25 to 30 members. Even with an upper limit of 30 it will only be possible to select a few of the many Canadians who could make a useful contribution to the work of the council.
One further word about the council. It will be noted that appointments may be for up to three years in duration. This could well mean that a number of appointments will be for less than three years, to permit rotation of members. It will also allow for the fact that some organizations may wish to change their representation more frequently than the maximum term provides. Some, for example, may want to be represented by an annually elected president. In any event the bill, I believe, furnishes sufficient flexibility to take care of most problems in this regard.
The house will naturally want to know when we plan to establish the new advisory council being proposed. Before appointing and convening this body it will be necessary to recruit staff and build up a departmental organization to carry out our part of the program. This will take some time, but we will press forward immediately, and when this phase has been completed we will be in a position to hold the first meeting of the national advisory council. I would sincerely hope that this process could be accomplished reasonably soon, thereby setting the course for the implementation of long range plans.
This is not to say, however, that in, the interim funds will not be made available for projects which may need immediate attention.
I have in mind, for example, further financial support which will be required in connection with Canada's efforts to obtain the winter Olympics in 1968. Another matter of some urgency is the fact that the British empire and commonwealth games association is looking to the government for financial support in connection with the games to be held in Perth, Australia, next year.
All these rather pressing problems will receive consideration by the government and will be dealt with while the over-all plan is being developed. There may be other ad hoc projects which will have to be considered prior to the first meeting of the new advisory council.

In any event, my department stands ready to do its utmost in meeting current needs and in seeing that everything possible is done to get this far reaching new venture off to a good start. I should like to thank hon. members for bearing with me through this rather extended explanation. I trust I have covered the major points of interest and I will, of course, be happy to go into further details when we reach the committee stage.

maintopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF ADVISORY COUNCIL ON FITNESS AND AMATEUR SPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank the minister at once for the lengthy statement he just made, not only regarding the principle of this legislation, but with respect to the various provisions of the bill before us. In his statement, the minister gave us a general idea of the manner in which this act will be administered.
All those who are either directly or indirectly interested in this important matter must be grateful to the minister for the information he supplied to the house.
It is essential, in my opinion, that we should know not only in a general way but also in some detail, the objects of this legislation, how it will be administered, and the manner in which the national advisory council will operate.
For this reason, I say to the minister that the information he just gave will be very valuable to us.
This bill has three purposes. 1. To encourage, promote and develop fitness and amateur sport. 2. To enter into an agreement with any province to provide for the payment of contributions towards the undertaking of programs designed to promote fitness and sport. 3. To provide for the setting up of a national advisory council on fitness and amateur sport.
This bill is not controversial and will not give rise to partisanship.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson), has made known to the house our stand on this important bill, and I have no intention of repeating what he said. It is for personal reasons and in my capacity as a private member that I am taking part in this debate.
This bill is not only good, it is essential. I am sure that all parties, indeed every hon. member will be in favour of the bill and will readily support it.
In this legislation, Mr. Speaker, we find two recurring words, fitness and sport. The two features of this bill are the promotion and the development of fitness and amateur sports.
Advisory Council on Sports
It is a sound piece of legislation for several reasons. First because it concerns more particularly our youth. I do not think one can put too much emphasis on the value of sports as an effective training for our youth.
The aim in sports is substantially the same as that in education. It is to develop the natural dispositions of the individual, to build his character, to strengthen his will and intelligence and to give him sounder judgment. But, I do also believe that sports, where practised in a sound and sensible way, can effectively contribute to the intellectual fitness and moral training of the individual.
I consider athletics as an excellent school for courage. The athlete is called upon to do his utmost, to concentrate all his efforts in order to achieve what he is aiming at.
He must often risk the fiercest impacts, ask of his body efforts which will leave him nearly exhausted, but above all he must work constantly at improving his performance because, of course, no one is born an athlete. Heredity is not of much consequence in this field and athletic ability is only the result of constant effort.
Success in sport is impossible without regular and constant repetition of exercises to develop muscles and reflexes, and that is done by hard training.
I have in mind a great athlete, the greatest, I think, in the field of hockey, Maurice Richard, whose brilliant career has warmed the heart of all his compatriots and indeed of every Canadian. But the triumphs he has known were made possible only by his determination, his steadfastness of purpose and his courage in bringing his art to perfection.
It was that kind of courage which enabled him to obtain the highest honours in the world of sports, and it is that same strength of character which must be developed by all athletes aspiring to success, especially those who want to imitate that great athlete.
I am also thinking of another athlete who won fame on the gridiron, another Montrealer, Phil Cornellier.
In the glorious era when the University of Ottawa won the Canadian football championship year after year, Cornellier was one of the brightest stars on the team. His speed, his running ability, his judgment, his power kicks, won the admiration of all those who saw him in action at the time. But his achievements did not stop there. I think his athletic training had much to do with his academic career, in which he later on obtained unlimited success. He was rector of the University of Ottawa, and dean of the faculties of
8838	HOUSE OF
Advisory Council on Sports philosophy and theology. He now lives as a simple Oblate father at the university after such a brilliant career.
In the second place, sports are a training school because they provide the opportunity to exercise self discipline. In a democratic country like ours the discipline necessary for the maintenance of order must be self inspired rather than imposed from outside.
It is said that President Lincoln, on entering an American hospital, collided with a young man who was quite in a hurry getting out. In fact, the president was knocked over and fell. As he was rising slowly, the young man said: "What on earth are you doing? Don't you see where you're going?" Then the president replied: "Young man, there is something wrong within you, in your inner self."
The society in which we live demands from the individual a greater measure of self control. Man must learn to bend his will and conform his actions to the needs of the common weal. In fact, his happiness and success in life are conditioned, to a large extent, by his ability to integrate himself in the life of the community.
In many ways, the practice of sports contributes to instil into the soul that internal discipline which is the best guarantee of success and happiness.
In order to succeed, an athlete should also be able to comply with the needs of concerted effort or team work. In many sports, like football, baseball and hockey, individual feats are less important to the success of a team than harmony and teamwork. Whatever his ability and his desire to shine individually, the athlete should be able to stand aside and co-ordinate his action with that of his teammates. To sum it up, he should make a personal sacrifice for the common benefit of the team.
The happy influence of sport in a young man's education is also evident in many other ways. Such activities stimulate self expression. Living long hours with his fellow athletes, talking and having fun together develop more relaxed personality and faster renewed self confidence. Teamwork and companionship train the young man in self expression and in giving the best of himself. Wherever it may be-at university, college, school, on public playing fields, or even in the great Canadian arenas, sport efficiently contributes to the training of tomorrow's leaders.
In Canada, team work has a particular significance, because it helps bring together


from all parts of our vast country athletes who represent the various nationalities and religions comprised in this nation. At a time where complete national unity is of such vital importance, sport can play a significant part as a means of goodwill and understanding.
I am thinking now of "Newsy" Lalonde, one of the greatest of his time, both on lacrosse fields and in hockey rinks. I recently read what he thinks of those with whom he contended. In a talk with the representative of a Canadian magazine, he had particular praise for his opponents. And the same thing happened when Maurice Richard and Gordie Howe made comments with regard to each other. They not only praised each other's achievements, but insisted on moral qualities.
Now, may I ask, how can prejudice and distrust subsist among young athletes brought together in daily life and making a common effort with the greatest and closest possible co-operation?
Inter-scholastic and amateur sports, which oppose teams of different parts of this country, bear the same good fruits.
I recall that several years ago, during the Alexander cup series between Valleyfield and Sydney, Valleyfield authorities organized a grand official reception for the visiting team. I am sure that those young athletes from Nova Scotia, some of whom perhaps were visiting the province of Quebec for the first time, went back home with a better understanding of their French speaking fellow-countrymen and with higher regard for them.
While it is true that clashes of opinion make for better understanding, I believe it is equally true that bodily clashes are often conducive to good will and mutual respect.
In time of peace as in time of war, a nation should be able to rely on a strong and healthy youth. In a rich and young country like ours, those who face life with strength can look forward to a bright future. Our boundless resources belong to the most aggressive and spirited people. They also belong to those who, among this new generation, will show strength, personality and initiative.
Those are a few of the reasons for which, I think, we should support this bill. They are also some of the reasons-there are many more-for which I believe this is an excellent measure.
I should not want to conclude on a discordant note, but may I draw to the attention

of this house an item in the Nouveau Journal of Saturday, September 23, 1961, under the by-line of Mr. Jacques Barrette. Let me quote only a few paragraphs of the article entitled:
Will the province of Quebec have its share?
With regard to everything taking place in the federal parliament, at Ottawa, the people of the province of Quebec remain prudent. They are not sure that they will receive their share from those parliamentarians who, more often than not, neglect our wonderful province. This is not chauvinistic, but a statement of fact.
And elsewhere:
One thing always puzzled us. How is it that no hockey team of the province of Quebec has ever been chosen to represent our country at Olympic games or world championships?
And finally, this last paragraph:
Last year, Hev. Father de la Sablonniere, s.j., director of the "Centre de lTmmaculee-Conception", made stirring representations to our governments with a view to securing substantial financial aid, without which the admirable work of those sports devotees is impossible. The "Reverend Father" had also proved unequivocally that the free time of our youth must be properly organized. The best way to achieve this is to get young people interested in sports.
I need not tell the house what place the "Centre des loisirs de lTmmaculee-Conception" occupies in Montreal sports under the leadership of its director, Father de la Sablonniere. Not only did he take particular interest in sports, but he also rendered tremendous service to our youth.
My colleague, the hon. member for La-fontaine (Mr. Ratelle), in whose constituency the "Centre des loisirs" is located, has time and again spoken about it in this house as outside.
I hope that Rev. Father de la Sablonniere's appeal will receive favourable consideration in the future.
Again, I could say something about recreation centres in the parish of St. John the Baptist and of St. Denis, in Laurier riding where tomorrow's youth is being developed, but unfortunately I do not have enough time.
I would only add that recreation centres are to be found everywhere in the province of Quebec and that a wonderful job is being performed there. I hope that, under this legislation, we shall be able to help these establishments as well as the young people who try to improve their bodies and their minds in those magnificent places.
I shall close my remarks with a simple comment, and a rather pleasant one. I thank the minister for having listened attentively to what I said.
Advisory Council on Sports
It is obvious that the minister will see to it that the act is administered with justice and fairness, whether through a national advisory council or through another body, for all groups, or associations which this legislation concerns.
Since this measure has been welcomed by all the members at the resolution stage and the bill before us will receive the unanimous approval of this house and since, in the administration thereof, there must be no "partisanship", in the broadest sense of the word, I am confident that the minister, through the government, by the well-advised selection of his advisory council, will see to it that the act is administered with justice and fairness throughout Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I intend to occupy even less time than is available before the luncheon adjournment. At the resolution stage the hon. member for Peterborough indicated clearly and ably why the members of this group intend to support this bill at the present stage and also at the ensuing stages.
I have only a few ideas to mention at this time. In the expenditure of this money on physical fitness and amateur sport I hope our government is going to realize the urgent need to develop an adequate number of leaders. Before we can actually have an effective national physical fitness and amateur sport program I believe we shall require tens of thousands more leaders than we now have in this particular field. I believe that one of the most important responsibilities in connection with the expenditure of this amount of money ought to be to prepare a program that will assure us of adequate leadership.
I hope the government is going to be much more successful in obtaining the co-operation of the ten provincial governments in this particular matter than they were in connection with the program of a number of years ago. At the time of the ending of that program only the government of the province of Saskatchewan was taking advantage of the assistance then available. I regret that at that time British Columbia curtailed this program to the point that it no longer participated.
I wish to raise these two points now. I note that the bill contains authority for the federal government to proceed on its own in the expenditure of this money. We all realize that under the terms of the British North America

The house resumed at 2.30 p.m.
Advisory Council on Sports Act, health and education come within the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces. Hitherto the provinces to a certain extent agreed to permit Ottawa also to participate in the development of good health in Canada. We have such things as a national hospital insurance program and grants for health. However, in the bill the government takes unto itself the authority to expend this $5 million a year without necessarily receiving the consent of the provincial or municipal authorities.
In the light of our experience with the pro-rec program I believe the attitude adopted may be wise indeed, in that it will enable this government to assist organizations and agencies within a province even though the provincial government may find itself unwilling to have any participation in the expenditure of this money. I hope all the provincial governments are going to recognize their responsibility and are going to help the minister more than they helped the then minister in the days of the pro-rec program.
I also note that the bill contains authority for an annual expenditure of $5 million. This provision is a bit unusual. It is something that we usually do not have in our legislation. The legislation usually merely establishes the authority and the machinery and then by way of annual estimate the House of Commons decides, on the advice of the government, how much it is going to allot to this particular program in each and every year. I know that the act as it is now presented is going to make it much easier for those responsible for planning to engage in long range planning, in that they are no longer dependent upon the House of Commons for their minimum annual revenue. However, it either carries on or initiates rather a departure from established custom, and it contains a certain danger. I should like the minister to tell us exactly what was the reason of the government for making the amount a part of the act, and making it an annual amount.
I hope the minister will also attempt to explain how the government hopes to enlist the aid of other levels of government. If we average this amount among our constituencies we find that it involves an expenditure of roughly $19,000 per constituency. Without the active team work of the other levels of government, $19,000 cannot very usefully be expended on this program in each and every constituency. The active participation of other levels of government will be urgently needed if we are to attain the aim indicated in this act.
At one o'clock the house took recess.
[Mr. Regier.l

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be able to take part in this important debate on sports. Sports that are properly conducted are very necessary for the youth of today, and extremely important to the present and future of Canada. This year 22 cents out of every dollar of our budget is spent on welfare. One sure way of cutting this down would be the proper training of youth.
It seems that the Olympic games are more in the limelight and receive more interest from the average Canadian than ever before. This is perhaps because of the sports pages of our newspapers, because the games are completely covered by these expert sports writers. Sports and competitions between countries can serve to promote good feelings if conducted in the right way, and I am sure that our sports writers have been and always will be of great help in this regard.
Mr. Speaker, the creed of the Olympic games has been mentioned previously, but I should like to repeat it. It is as follows:
The Important thing in the Olympic games is not winning but taking part. The essential thing in life is not conquering but fighting well.
The motto is simply citius, altius, fortius, which means "higher, swifter, stronger". Neither the creed nor the motto can be properly carried out under the strain of present-day Olympics without the best coaching and direction, and I believe this should be the concern of the federal government.
Grown Canadians have a great variety of sports that will keep them in shape. They can take part in golf, badminton, tennis, softball, ping pong, swimming, boating, fishing, hunting, archery, trap shooting, hiking, mountain climbing, riding, flying, skiing, skating, curling and bowling. Most of these sports are available and are being carried out by a great number of Canadians in all parts of Canada. If one does not care to spend money on any of the above to build up his strength and keep fit, he can get good results by walking or by doing the daily dozen every morning.
Mr. Speaker, it seems that our most important duty to Canadians in the line of sports is to have a program of sports training for our youth. Children should be exposed to sports at a very early age, and should receive proper instruction and supervision. Too many of our children are left to fend for themselves They grow up without proper training, and without this training many of them later on in life help to swell the ranks of the unemployed. The youth of today are the leaders

and builders of our Canada of tomorrow. A proper training system should be set up as soon as possible.
Back in 1946 I suggested to Mr. Douglas Grimston, president of the Canadian amateur hockey association, that a school of coaching should be established in Canada by the federal government, and that the government should have a department to promote and finance sports in Canada. Mr. Ken McConnell, then sports editor of the Vancouver Province, agreed to this plan but said I was 15 years too soon. It seems that Mr. McConnell was right when he said 15 years, and I am very pleased that this government is now taking action.
At that particular time I talked this plan over with Mr. Summerfield, sports editor of the Nanaimo Free Press, and also Bill Phillips, who is now the arena manager in New Westminster and was at that time. Of course, as everyone knows who follows hockey, he was at one time a national league hockey player. Mr. Phillips endorsed that plan, and the suggestion that I take it up with the government. As a matter of fact Mr. Grimston asked me to go east to the meeting of the Canadian amateur hockey association, but I was unable to do so at that time.
I am going to take the liberty of reading from an official hockey program of the 1946-47 season. This is a program published by the Queen's Park arena, New Westminster. The editorial is entitled "Hockey News" and reads:
Bus Matthews of Nanaimo, one of the coast's most ardent hockeyists, both as a player and coach of young players, expresses a thought which carries so much merit, it can not very well be ditched and forgotten.
Hockey today is big business in the east and is becoming big business on the Pacific coast, and, with the expansion of the game the cry is going to be, more and more, for hockey material. Canada has been and will for a long time continue to be the proving ground for young hockey players who will carry the load in the future in top brackets. How these youngsters are trained and developed will determine the greatness of future hockey. The percentage of boys starting the game who make the top is very small; according to Bus, the percentage could be very greatly increased if proper methods of training them, by men themselves properly trained in coaching, were adopted.
Bus maintains that there are only a few men living today who have the knowledge to set down in print the fundamental principles of good hockey play and the right methods of teaching these principles, and while they are available to the game they should be brought together as a body and set up as the authority defining good instruction, good methods of teaching and qualifications of men to become teachers of our future hockey stars. A few years from now, these men will be gone and the opportunity lost.
I might explain that at that time I suggested the government should get a group of these leaders in sports together for a period of say two weeks. Stenographers would
Advisory Council on Sports be provided to take down what was said, and each man could contribute from his experience of the phase of the game in which he was most interested, defensive play, attack and so on. I mentioned at that time the name of Lester Patrick as one of the hockey experts who might be invited to such a meeting. He and others like him have had years of experience in training young hockey players and shaping them from the raw material. We have already lost Mr. Lester Patrick, and we have also lost that famous player and coach Mr. Dick Irwin.
Men such as these have an experience which covers many decades of hockey. Their knowledge of the game goes back over the time when we in Canada played seven man hockey, six man hockey and five man hockey. Many people in Canada do not know that there was a league which played five man hockey. I think this new council might well consider the suggestion that men of this calibre should be invited to a conference to give us all the benefit of the knowledge they have gained; and I have in mind all sports, not just hockey.
Today the big leagues want players who are complete in all respects; they do not want to have to teach them anything. That is the work of the coaches. I do not want to give the impression that I have in mind only professional hockey. I do not think it should be confined to professional hockey. I believe it should be extended to help young Canadians who are on their way in the business world as a means of building up their minds and improving their bodies.
In July of 1958 a softball game was played in Hull between members of parliament and members of the House of Commons staff. I forget all those who were there, but I am sure the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Taylor) and the hon. member for Waterloo North (Mr. Weichel) took part. I do not remember now who won the game, but I think it was the staff. Lester Patrick, Newsy Lalonde, Fred Taylor and others were there as guests. We had a get together afterward at which Lester Patrick, Mr. Lalonde and others were asked to say a few words. When my own turn came to speak I stressed the importance of the government setting up a department to help promote sports, and said I thought a coaching school should be established. Hon. members will well understand my pleasure when the Prime Minister announced the other day that such a program would be put into operation by the government.
As reported on page 120 of Hansard for January 20, 1959, the hon. member for Waterloo North suggested that a ministry of sport

Advisory Council on Sports should be established. If hon. members turn to page 1037 of Hansard of February 16, 1959 they will find that the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard proposed the setting up of a sports council. I wish to congratulate these two hon. members and other members of the house who have worked so hard, informally, in the promotion of these ideas. There was a committee formed for this purpose, and the hon. members I have mentioned, together with others, contributed a great deal to the idea which is now being put into practical form.
I support Bill No. C-131. When a member supports a bill in the House of Commons I believe, Mr. Speaker, that he should put his reasons for doing so on record. The following are my reasons. Statements have been made that Canada is a nation of weaklings; that people who are just spectators and who do not play games are weaklings. I do not agree with this, and I do not take such statements for granted.
Let us not sell Canadian youth short. I know that we have in Canada many very fine young people who will go a long way in business and sport as the years go by. Looking around today we see that our young boys are growing broader, taller and stronger. I do not like to hear people say that we are a nation of weak people, and I would not advise anyone to step up to many of these young fellows and say that. It reminds me of a story of a man in Texas. When he had had a few drinks he looked around and said "I can lick anyone in this bar". No one said anything; he was a pretty big man. After a while he turned around and said "I can lick anyone in Texas." Still nobody took him on. Finally, after one or two more drinks, the visitor declare "I can lick anyone in the United States". At that point a little fellow stood up, took off his glasses, and knocked him down. When the challenger finally came around he murmured "I guess I took in too much territory".
Taking part in sports is important for the building of the mind as well as of the body. I coached sports for a number of years, and I found that the important thing was to get the player to think. A player who thinks becomes twice as valuable. I have coached many players who I am sure would have gone a long way in hockey if they had continued in the game. I have kept records of many hundreds of my young players, and I go over them from time to time. There is not one of those boys who is not doing very well today. Two of them, for example, quit and went fishing. They now own commercial fishing boats worth between $75,000 and $100,000 each. Others have become electrical


contractors, clothing store owners, pharmacists, dentists and doctors-and I am talking now about the stars who quit the game, people who could really have gone places in the sport itself. However, they decided they would seek careers in business or in the professions rather than in commercial sport.
As I was saying, it is important that a player should learn to think. It is harder to think, to really concentrate, than it is to run, jump or skate. If you cannot get your players to think you will certainly never have top grade players. I remember I was once in a rink at the start of a season when Mr. Lester Patrick was looking over one of his clubs. I said "Lester, you certainly have a fine bunch of strong players. They should go a long way." This was on the west coast. He said "I have not got one man on that team who will ever get to the national hockey league". I said "They look good to me". He said "They can stickhandle, check and skate, but they have not got it above the ears". Unless a player has it above the ears he will not go far in professional sport today.
Today, when we worry so much about what our young people are doing, we should certainly see that their bodies are developed. We should make sure, also, that we have coaches who will develop their minds. If I were going to make a quotation at this time I would say "Men who do not think are the weaklings of today".
People who observe sport have always been important to me, and when I coach I use sports writers as a source of information. A sports writer has to meet a deadline. He has to examine the performance of players and scrutinize the games closely in order to have something about which to write. The only way he can do so is by thinking. The day following a game I always made it a point to talk to the news writers and get their views. As a result I was often able to learn things which were a means of improving my players.
A good coach is, in a sense, a mirror and by that I mean a mirror that is accurate, that is not cracked or distorted. There is no one in this building who would accept as gospel truth the reflection given by a mirror with a tendency to distort. Such a mirror would be thrown out of the window. A good coach requires the ability to accurately reflect the potentiality of his team. I know of a famous golfer in the United States who every once in a while would ask some minor pro to follow him about and watch him play, and advise if he was doing anything wrong. Some pros protested that the player knew more about golf than they would ever know, but he pointed out that it was impossible for him to drive or putt a ball and look in a mirror

at the same time. He asked them to reflect back to him accurately the way he played the game. I use this illustration to indicate that a good coach must accurately reflect the ability of his team. If he is a good coach he must be of assistance to the boys.
One could speak at great length about coaching, but I shall content myself with telling one small story. The cousin of a player in a small town, a young lad who had been in reform school, expressed an interest in sports. I spoke to the young man about having his cousin come down to play, and eventually spoke to the mother of the former inmate of a reform school about the boy participating in juvenile sport. I expressed my interest in having him join us. The mother explained that he did not wish to play because he was aware that the boys knew he had stolen and thought they would not want him in the locker room. I explained that I had spoken to the boys and that he would be welcome. After persuasion the young man came and played hockey. In speaking to his mother at a later date she said that had it not been for that opportunity to participate in sports the boy would have run away and perhaps again taken up a life of crime. That young man is now married, with two children, and is purchasing his own home. If it had not been for the opportunity I have mentioned he might well not have been in that fortunate position today.
I have told that story to illustrate how important it is that the council ensure that good coaches are obtained. I think it is most important also that the council give consideration to assisting young Indian boys especially by encouraging them to participate in lacrosse. I urge the council to endeavour to have lacrosse returned to its former standing in the Olympic games.
I hope the council when in operation will be careful in making grants. I do not believe grants should be made to professional teams. I know of a very good orchestra that made application for a Canada Council grant. The orchestra received the answer that the council only assisted orchestras that had reached professional status. Probably the members of the Canada Council know more about music than I do, but I disagree with their basic policy. I maintain that if an orchestra has reached professional standing it should not be given grants.
Similarly, I do not see why grants should be given by the sports council to people who have reached professional status. I believe they should be given only to amateur sports that do so much to build healthy minds and bodies among young Canadians. I suggest assistance in the establishment of playing fields and ice surfaces. I know of a number
Advisory Council on Sports of clubs that would be interested in participating in a program of that type. Very careful attention will have to be paid to the selection of the members of the council, and equally careful attention will have to be paid by the council in the selection of coaches if a school is set up.
Sports are important to all countries, and one could discuss this topic for hours. Last year I was in attendance at the interparliamentary union conference in Tokyo, where I stayed at the New Japan hotel. I was surprised to receive a telephone call advising me that Prince Takeda, the president of the national skating union of Japan, wished to see me. I said I would be interested in meeting him, and although I suspected at first that I was being kidded an appointment was made for 2.30 the next afternoon. I was pleased when the prince arrived with his secretary and we discussed sports, including hockey. As hon. members know a Japanese team participated in the Olympic games last year and did a fine job, although they achieved no great success. Much credit should be given to them for the spirit they brought to the game. The prince has requested that I send him a film illustrating lacrosse about which I told him. He is of the opinion that it might become a popular game in Japan.
During our visit we wore badges indicating that we were from Canada. At a reception one night I met a young Japanese boy who said, "Me Broda". I found out that he played hockey and knew of Turk Broda, who was his hero. The badge brought me many encounters. Two young Japanese connected with newspaper and radio spent most of an evening with me. All they wished to talk about was sports including baseball and hockey. I assure hon. members that Canada is held in high regard by the people of Japan.
Many interesting articles concerning sports appear in newspapers from time to time. In the February, 1960 issue of The Legionary Mr. Lome Manchester, in an article entitled "A Bad Case of "Spectatoritis" stated:
Thousands of youngsters under the guidance of Canadian Legion branches are engaged in regular league schedules throughout the country .. . Many youngsters are also getting their first introduction to ''Operation Star-Shooter", the Canadian Legion's program of carefully worked out gymnastic exercises designed to improve the physical fitness of our young people.
The Legion branches across Canada are sponsoring sports. Every branch in my constituency sponsors a team or buys equipment. All are anxious to do their part for the future of Canadian sports. Before I left home I was approached by the new Legion branch. They are interested in knowing if any assistance could be given in the establishment of

Advisory Council on Sports a small ice surface. They have a number of boys' teams. They wish information and assistance in the form of a grant, and would be willing to participate in financing the necessary balance. I am proud to say that every service club in my constituency sponsors a team or provides uniforms or equipment for hockey and lacrosse teams. This is a wonderful thing, and I think a similar situation prevails across Canada.
Within these small groups are found some of the finest coaches in Canada. They donate their services without charge and desire no remuneration. Men who are prepared to do that are coaches of the best type. When the school of coaching is established, and when information and ideas on coaching are finally collected and drafted, I suggest that these men be informed. They should be given every assistance and all the information that will be of help to them in their coaching.
I spoke a few moments ago about lacrosse, a wonderful game that is much misunderstood. For years it was represented as brutal and sensational, but when properly presented it is known as a game of skill. It is widely played in England and Australia. Interestingly enough, more lacrosse is played in colleges in the United States than is played in Canada, and that in spite of the fact that lacrosse is historically Canada's national game. I have here a short dispatch from London which reads as follows:
Canada's historic sport, lacrosse, is becoming increasingly popular in Britain. Two London schools have now included lacrosse in their curriculum, and more are expected to join.
In other words, our game is to be brought up to the status it should have, because it is number one in sports as a mind and body builder. It has been proven by professors who have investigated the matter that lacrosse is number one as a body builder and mind builder. One junior lacrosse team in a league in Vancouver was composed entirely of what we sometimes refer to now as dead end kids. I got to know many of the boys and I can tell you that there were some bad actors among them, but they went on to play senior lacrosse, and played the finest lacrosse in Canada. Those boys were all salvaged and trained to be good Canadians by a coach who was not a professional but who did a tremendous job and prevented those dead end kids from being a charge on the rest of the people of Canada.
I could read other articles about the progress of lacrosse in the United States. No doubt the committee will be made aware of all this information. I have all the statistics as to injuries which show why lacrosse is considered to be safer than hockey and even safer than baseball in some respects. These


statistics have been collected over a period of years, and I will be very glad to supply them to the minister because I know he will make good use of them.
It may be that first of all the board will make a survey right across Canada to get suggestions and advice from people who have been engaged for years in the sports field. There are many members of the house who are well qualified to do this work and who would know how to get in touch with people to obtain this information. I know these men could supply good advice on the subject.
I could continue but I know there are other members who wish to speak on this very important subject. There is one point I should like to make in conclusion. I am afraid I will not be able to make it, because apparently I need a little more coaching; I have mislaid my note. I should like to mention that this year the British Columbia senior women's softball championship was won by a Duncan team coached by Duff Chaster. He is not a professional coach, and this is a wonderful achievement for a team in its first year of competition.
Various championships in all kinds of sports have been won by teams in my constituency. However, I do not want to take any more time, and I will simply say that I am very happy that we have reached the ponit of taking action with regard to this matter that is so important for the future of our children and the people of Canada generally. I know the minister will do a tremendous job. I know he is most interested in the subject. I noted a short time ago that due to conditions beyond his control he lost five or six suits. In sports when a sponsor loses a lot of money he is referred to as having lost his shirt. I hope the minister will not allow this committee to get out of control and lose his shirt.

Mr. Speaker, my first remarks, of course, must be to congratulate the minister on the introduction of what is perhaps in this session the first piece of legislation uncontested and unanimously supported, not only by members of the house but by the people of the country at large. This is certainly to his credit. The demand or desire for the legislation is quite apparent. It was introduced in the form of a private bill initially, and has since received support from newspaper columnists. Credit is due to a great many people for their efforts which have culminated in the bill now before us, even to those members of parliament who have taken part in some athletic endeavour, either in hockey or on the baseball

diamond. If their inability to play these games is any indication, surely this bill to improve their physical fitness is certainly necessary.
One cannot and should not be facetious about legislation involving such an important principle, and involving $5 million to be taken from the public treasury. While I accept all the arguments as to the necessity for the bill, perhaps not only at this point but in the committee stage we might look at how these worthy principles and objectives are going to be achieved. How are we going to spend the $5 million; to what purpose; who will receive the money, and what are going to be the problems of the administrative council on whom in the final analysis the success or failure of the legislation will depend?
As many speakers who have preceded me have said, the bill has three principal purposes; first, to improve the physical fitness of the people of Canada as a whole; second, to aid amateur sport and, third, to assist Canada's competing athletes in international events. I suggest to you, sir, and to the minister that all these are separate objectives, though interrelated. None the less, at this stage and,in the committee we must assign ourselves the task of recognizing that each requires individual study if we are to achieve any degree of success in attaining our objectives.
We have read the bill, and have observed the nine points which form the basis of the regulations, and the principles as to how the moneys are to be assigned under working agreements with individuals, organizations and with the provinces. The first question we must ask ourselves is, what control will the council have when these moneys pass from their hands.
To take a specific example, let us say that province A is provided with X dollars. How are we going to be assured that the objectives outlined in the legislation will be pursued by province A? How are we going to avert any possibility that these moneys will perhaps go toward some other objective which is not indicated or intimated in the terms of the legislation? To a large degree, of course, this is going to be a responsibility of the council itself, the administrative body.
Second, in addition to establishing a group of fundamental principles and making an assessment of all the essential needs in respect of coaching in schools and improvement of facilities, we must assure ourselves that somehow we create a desire within Canadians to want to be physically fit and to take a greater interest in amateur sport, because if the desire is not present there is no purpose in providing facilities.
At this point it amuses me a little to listen to some of my colleagues who, in describing
Advisory Council on Sports the advantages of helping amateur sport, cannot resist the temptation to kick what they describe as professionalism in sport. I think it should be clearly understood that many of the youngsters we see on the playing fields are emulating the Jackie Parkers, Babe Ruths and other major sports heroes. It is from these professionals that they get the desire to become athletes. I am not advocating that money be contributed to assist professionalism, but I suggest that in the end this legislation will not be successful unless professional sport and professional organizations carry on as they have done in past years.
I can recall having taken part in the first large scale attempt by the west to win a well known sporting event, the Grey cup in 1948. The effort was not that of a group of professionals. It was a community endeavour by a group of people who got together and decided that the then little known pastime of football should be made a national classic. It was not any paid group of promoters who were involved, rather, it was community spirit which made it so successful. We took our cowboys, our Indians and our football players and captured the imagination of the Canadian people, thus making this sporting event what it is today.
Here again I must relate the importance of this bill to other aspects of the subject. Take hockey, baseball or football, and you can see the advantages of professionals and amateurs working together to achieve a better physical condition for the Canadian public. What concerns me, though, is that Canadians today, unfortunately, are gradually becoming a nation of spectators rather than competitors. I hope this is a place where the bill perhaps makes its greatest contribution. As I said at the outset, we must be absolutely certain we press steadily forward to achieve this objective. The council will have many responsibilities and many problems. Let me try to tell the council what I hope it will not do because, after all, in the final analysis success or failure is going to rest upon this.
First of all, I would hope they would not contribute moneys to purely organizational or office work which is involved in developing a sport. I would hope that the moneys would be assigned to the root of the problem, to the youngsters. Second, I would hope the council would not assign moneys to any organization which had a history of not being able to help itself. I listened to one of my distinguished colleagues who made a great contribution to the debate, but in the first six minutes he had spent the $5 million. I heard also suggestions to the effect that a dollar

Advisory Council on Sports should be paid here or $50 there, and that this was going to help amateur sports and physical fitness.
I agree that these are indeed worthy causes, but we must remember that if the $5 million is going to be spent wisely it is going to have to be spread amongst a great many individuals and a great many interests in the sporting field. I would hope, therefore, that the council would try to assist those people who are prepared to help themselves, and let the contributions in terms of dollars be measured accordingly. Any sporting organization-you and I have belonged to many of them-which is not prepared to get off the ground itself and do something for itself will never survive, no matter what government hand-out is given. The point I make, therefore, is that there should be a careful assessment of what the organization has done in the past, how it is prepared to assist in its own endeavour, and then whether government aid can give it enough help to get beyond the point of being mediocre.
Then we come to another problem. How do you reconcile the differences that may exist between those people who believe in physical fitness as an end in itself and those well organized groups of people involved in amateur sports, in so far as representation on the council is concerned? How are you going to distinguish where the money is to go, and who is going to get how much? This is going to be another major problem. It is a platitude and a generality, I recognize, to say that one area of sport should receive a benefit while another does not. There is a point here, Mr. Speaker, and the bill clearly sets out that there are these two principles. The one must not in any way become the poor relation of the other. The council must, therefore, be selective on the basis that there will be those who can speak as advocates for both.
I should like to make one or two other suggestions. The council will have its problems, but after all if this legislation passes the house our advice to it will be of little value. It is only now while the bill is in this stage that we can make definite recommendations. I would hope the council would not attempt to spend its money in sending, for example, vast arrays of coaches or escort parties abroad with our athletes. This again is something that is important. I would hope that the money would be spent in developing athletes basically in Canada, and let these other organizations take up these additional costs. I would hope the money would be utilized for some of those things which have been suggested here, but we must place


priorities on them and see that we do not spend so little on each that there is no real effect in any particular area of sport. >
As I said at the beginning, I think the important thing is to try to get a philosophy of mind in our young people so that they will want to compete. This is the biggest problem the council will have. I have heard from a friend of mine about youngsters who were discouraged from competing in the vast areas which could be devoted to some form of recreation. I suggest to you, sir, that keeping in mind the variety of interests which today compete for the time of our young people, we must map out a plan that will encourage them to reach the standards we hope will be attained as a result of this bill. If Canada intends to put itself on international display in the Olympics and other world events, I believe we should be improving the ability of our youngsters to compete by providing them with the facilities they require. We should set up co-ordinating bodies to ensure that one organization does not overlap on the functions of another organization. This is another area in which the council can well assist, not only through its administrative responsibilities but through the funds it has to administer.
I suggest, therefore, that in making an assessment of the problems you must first of all make a review of the facilities that exist in Canada to determine the areas requiring the most help. Only from this point can we make a successful start.
Finally, sir, I should like to make one other suggestion involving two points. It has been said, I believe by the minister, that it is not the intention to include under this bill any funds that could be utilized for capital costs for national events that may come to Canada, such as the Pan-American games, the British empire games or any of the Olympic games. I think this is indeed a wise move, and not because I come from a city which hopes to be the host for the winter Olympic games of 1968. If you take the moneys available under this bill and assign them to the larger international events it means that the entire program will suffer. In fact it will be disrupted, because all the funds will be required for these three major events I have men tioned. In this way the funds needed to stimulate physical fitness and amateur sport will be lost. I was happy, therefore, to hear the minister make that point very clearly, that this money may be used to help the athlete prepare for the Olympic games, but it is not intended that it should be used for capital costs in connection with those games.
The second point, sir, involves the two booklets produced by the armed services known as 5BX and 10BX, in the war against

obesity in the services. I think many of us in this chamber might consider them as required reading for ourselves. These two booklets have become, in fact, Canadian best sellers, with sales totalling something over a quarter of a million. I would hope that the funds derived from the sale of those booklets would not go back into the general revenue fund. I would hope rather that, because of the importance of the work these people have already accomplished in the field of physical fitness, these funds could be used to encourage them to go into other areas as yet unexplored. I believe this is the greatest single contribution that any government agency has made to date in helping to assist in the national problem of reaching some level of physical fitness.
So, Mr. Speaker, I close as I began, by congratulating the minister in making the first step an important one. Second, I wish to state my belief that the council has indeed a real job in making this bill work, function and become successful. Third, I suggest that the council should attend to the problem of creating the desire in addition to the facilities so that our young people may enjoy physical fitness. Fourth, I would remind them that they have a dual responsibility, both in the field of physical fitness and of course amateur sport. Fifth, I would hope that in every area, whether it be in physical fitness or amateur sport, the professional and the amateur alike realize the vast potential that is available to them in the playing fields and the skating rinks; for here the real athletes are to be found. Here are the youngsters who will represent us in future years. Indeed, I suggest that here in fact is the future of Canada.
