Mr. Speaker, it is very difficult to follow such eminent speakers as those we have heard this afternoon. I should also like to congratulate the Minister of National Health and Welfare for bringing this important measure into the House of Commons. I might start off by saying that I come from a town that is well known for its athletics, both in the professional and amateur fields.
However, I should like to confine my remarks to the amateur field. I might say that this bill should be channelled to the masses if we are to have competitors in the future. We cannot merely buy championships. We cannot merely take a hockey team, spend $50,000 and send them over to Germany or to Russia in order to meet someone. I think the $5 million we are allocating today should be spread out across the country.
It disturbed me somewhat in the last week when I noticed that in some of their articles the newspapermen were saying that it was
Advisory Council on Sports time for Canada to flex its muscles. To me it seemed that they were trying to play down the bill. I think it is a great step in fostering the development of young people in the country, but it should not start when the boy is 18 or 19 years old, with a view to sending him to the Olympic games or to the world hockey championships. It should start in the homes by the parents encouraging their children to participate in active sports. I know that some parents do not wish this participation. They wish their children to go ahead and be scholastic in their ability. However, a little playing never hurt anyone.
In federal politics you should not talk about the provinces or the municipalities, because the British North America Act prevents you from getting into the school systems. But unless the school systems of the country- public schools, high schools and colleges-[DOT] get behind this physical fitness and amateur athletics bill, I do not think it will get off the ground; for the coaching that we are striving to spread across the country must come and be taught to boys all across the country. I think it is very important that the Minister of National Health and Welfare talk to his provincial colleagues so they can encourage the development of amateur athletics through the education system and so that we shall indeed be trying to teach boys from grade V up to adulthood.
There has been some talk about professional entrepreneurs coming under this type of bill. I do not think we have much to fear on that score. The amateur athletic unions in Canada, such as the Olympic association of Canada, have been well organized for years. Through their representations I am sure they will help this council to beware of professionalism, although professionalism is not a dirty word. Some few years ago I happened to be a professional athlete, and I may say that professional athletes are fairly good types in developing coaching in the country I would not want the minister to set up a coaching system in Ottawa by means of which you would bring only a few people from across the country to coaching school. I would rather see a mobile coaching staff go across the 10 provinces and set up regional schools at given dates so that a larger group of people could come and be helped in this way. Rather than having two or three people sent from Vancouver to Ottawa, I would rather see a coaching school of instructors go to Vancouver and have 50 people or 60 people participate.
In the western world, as I see it today, we go in for a good deal of glamour. It will be noticed that after the Olympic competitions in the past several years, everyone in the United States, Canada and the western world

Advisory Council on Sports wants to be a sprint champion. They forget about other non-glamorous sports that could be taken up. The Russians have won a large number of points in gymnastics and fencing and what might be termed back room sports. I think if we start to encourage our children who cannot be one hundred yard sprinters in 9.6 seconds to get into some other things by mass participation, we shall eventually have a great deal to look forward to in the future.
With regard to the grants indicated in the bill, I think the minister should be very cautious with regard to whom he gives money. I know there are in the country a great many people who are looking for assistance, but as was indicated by the hon. member for Calgary South, those people who cannot help themselves usually will not get off the ground by means of the great white father from Ottawa coming down and giving them some extra money.
At this point I might indicate the job that police associations, service clubs and sports organizations are doing across this country. I think they should continue to do this job because it is the basic fundamental of amateur sport. I refer to people wanting to get out and play and help the children all the time.
I would also talk to the minister with regard to what I would call socialites in sports. As indicated by the hon. member for Calgary South, when Canada sends 20 athletes to the Olympic games we seem to find that, having regard to our way of life, they must have 10 coaches to go with them. When Australia sent people to the commonwealth games a few years ago they sent some 90 athletes but only 10 coaches. We find that politics are played in many associations. I would make the council aware of the politics that are played in associations across the country.
As to the surveys that are indicated in the bill, I think surveys should be made of the facilities that are required across the country both in relation to coaching and physical requirements. Unfortunately we in the northern part of the western hemisphere have long winters. I think we should look into the possibility of capital cost expenditures in co-operation with the provinces and the municipalities in connection with the creation of field housing facilities such as those in existence in the United States for all-round training in a vast number of sports.
I think this bill will be widely accepted across the country. I do not think any politics will be played. However, I stress to the minister the point that this money should be spent wisely. As indicated by hon. members who have preceded me, if we are going to have the winter Olympic games in this country I do not think this money should


be spent for the purpose of building facilities for those games. This money should be used to foster the development of fitness and amateur sport in the country by mass participation. I stress to the minister the importance of getting in touch with his colleagues the health and education ministers of the provinces, so they in turn can sell the program through the schools. I am sure the minister is planning some literature to be handed out for this purpose.
I should like to take this opportunity to congratulate the amateur athletic associations in the country which for the past many years have been struggling to get into international competition. I know that I have been called on to donate to these organizations, as have many others. I should also like to point out to this council that something should be put into this bill which will allow the council itself to accept moneys from organizations that wish to help to develop amateur sport. In other words, if we are to make grants to Olympic teams to go over and compete in games in Tokyo or in Helsinki, I am sure the minister will find that there are many people who are willing to put up their dollars in order to help Canada in this respect. I think the bill should stress physical fitness for amateur athletes on a mass participation basis and we should not get down to specialization, for only through mass participation can we produce champions, which might not be in 1968 but it will be some time in the 1970's.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to participate in this discussion at this time, and my contribution will be brief. Many hon. members, including the hon. member for Hamilton South (Mr. McDonald), are far better qualified than I to discuss this subject and have already given some very thoughtful and helpful advice to the council. Without going over the ground that has already been covered, I should like to offer this one suggestion to the council. In my view the whole purpose of this legislation will be accomplished if the notion I have in mind comes about.
Clearly Canada, due to geographic and many other conditions, is not, even in the most optimistic person's mind, likely to become a front runner and top-flight contender in the Olympics of future years. We have, relatively speaking, a limited population and growth potential. We should face that fact, and one of the tasks I hope this council will undertake is to approach the various provinces and the various areas of this country and try in a co-operative way to achieve a fairly well planned cross-section of athletic endeavour.

This point was touched upon by the hon. member for Hamilton South. We can envisage universities in one area of the country concentrating on swimming and related activities, others concentrating on track and field events, others on skiing, others on gymnastics, fencing and the other sports which make up the whole Olympics calendar.
A certain amount of this has taken place naturally, it seems to me. I refer to McGill, Carleton University and Ottawa University. These are universities which are located close to adequate, and in fact very excellent skiing facilities. It seems to me that if the council can encourage this type of specialization and encourage universities or groups of universities, high schools, as the hon. member mentioned, and even the public school system we could develop coaching to such a degree that we would produce results in a very few years.
Most universities, apart from the few specializations I have mentioned, have made some outstanding contributions. Certainly Bruce Kidd, potentially the world's greatest distance runner, is an example of the case in point where proper encouragement and coaching is available. Another example that comes to mind of a small university establishing a reputation for itself is St. Francis Xavier University in Nova Scotia. I think that is an example of what I have in mind operating in a very successful way.
A few years ago that university brought Don Loney, who was a former professional football player with the Ottawa Rough Riders, to that university. He provided the university with the elements of a first-rate coaching staff. The institution has concentrated its athletic endeavours in that direction and as a result it has, I believe, the reputation of being the No. 1 football university in the maritime provinces, if not in eastern Canada.
It seems to me this concept should be extended possibly on a provincial basis, but certainly on a geographic basis. As I said when I rose to speak, if there is some movement and development in this direction this legislation will have justified itself beyond all our expectations.

assist players and athletes generally should be concentrated on the phase when our young people are beginning to develop their talents and abilities. I feel certain that this measure can be the
means of adding years to the lives of our
people and of adding more life to their years.
During my earlier years I had the experience of being an instructor in physical culture. Many people in my area could, I know, vouch for the truth of the statement I have made.
While the resolution and the bill make reference to "encouragement of physical fitness and sports" and while I have played many games for many years and enjoy them still and agree that there is much benefit to be gained from them, I nevertheless intend at this time to stress the need and the value of fitness for all regardless of how it is acquired rather than limiting my remarks at this stage to the benefits accruing to those who may participate in sports. I was particularly impressed by the remarks of the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Smith) who referred to the benefits that have been and no doubt will continue to ge gained from participation in the 5-BX and 10-BX programs.
I suggest that something continued along that line and broadened to include all the people of Canada might perhaps be of greater benefit than just to train athletes. Since I have been here as the representative of the people of my area in the parliament of Canada I have often thought that the most important contribution I might make would be to do or say something which would encourage the people of our country to follow such a course as is being advocated today. I spoke on this subject in the house on June 22, 1960, as recorded on page 5262 of Hansard. If I may, I should like to review a few of the remarks I made at that time.
May I say that it is my intention to speak about and to attempt to place special emphasis upon the need and the part that a physical fitness program encouraged from the federal level could play in working toward such a goal of improved health. I feel that there are practically unlimited possibilities in this field. I feel that I should at this time also acknowledge that it is generally recognized that the responsibility for this matter of physical fitness falls under the jurisdiction of the provincial authority, but I have long felt that more encouragement should be given from the federal level to encourage and assist the provincial governments, and in turn, the local municipal governments and the people themselves, in a program which would broaden and intensify their efforts in this regard.

I am one of those who believe that health and strength is just as valuable and important to the average businessman and other people as it is to the athlete, and that the same things

which the athlete does in a somewhat modified form would also promote strength and health for the one who may not wish to participate in organized sports.

I should like also to point out that the need for a physical fitness program on a national scale is becoming increasingly more important in this day and age when men are devising mechanical ways of doing the work which they did by hand in days gone by. As a result of the increasing nervous strain caused by the pace at which we are moving today I predict that there will be an ever increasing need in the years to come for something to take the place of the work that our bodies were intended by nature to perform.
And finally:
... I should like to take a moment to point out the tremendous benefit that could come to the people of Canada from a dollar and cents standpoint if a concerted effort were made to sponsor a health program which would be dominion wide and in which physical fitness would play a prominent part. I feel this to be especially important at this time since the government has become responsible for the health insurance of the people. An ounce of prevention to my mind is worth any number of pounds of cure. I therefore suggest that the government give most serious consideration to the advisability of encouraging some such program.
I know it is not going to be an easy thing to sell to all the people of our country the idea of keeping fit. In my earlier years I had trouble selling it even to my own family. But as the years have passed by my son now in his twenties finds that his father, who is well on in his fifties, can quite easily set the pace for him still. When my daughters see their mother in her fiftieth year wearing the same size clothes and dancing with the same enthusiasm and ease as she did when she was twenty, I find it becoming a powerful stimulus for them to strive toward that goal which we have attempted to set for them.
I do not say this arrogantly or boastfully. I say it because it is a fact and in the hope that it may prove an inspiration for other people. I know that many people dislike doing any more work than they have to. They seem to feel that the pinnacle of achievement is to get to the place where they do not have to work. I am prepared to agree with the statement that has been made in the house on many occasions, that you cannot legislate virtue. I can think of no more worth-while thing for any government to do.

This was in Montreal. Another example along the same line but having to do with some of the other points I tried to bring out, is the experience I had in the prize ring in my early years as a boxer. I am thinking of the man who gave me the most difficult battle I ever had. He beat me the first time; 3 obtained a draw on our second meeting, and I beat him on the third meeting. However, that man died about ten years ago. I also have in mind two other men who were outstanding baseball players in our district. They have both died. These three men were all a little heavier than I was when they were at their best, but when they died they were about 50 pounds overweight. They died when they were still young men. As I have said, this proves that we perhaps eat too much and we eat things that are not good for us. We drink too much, too.
May I say, too, that when I came down here as a member I endeavoured to revive the custom of playing a few games of baseball, and to encourage some of the boys to try to get in condition. I knew what had happened here, and I knew of the tragic occurrence during a game being played here. Some of my well meaning friends in the house suggested that I should act my age; that I should not make any attempt to re-organize the games at this time. I did make the statement then that I thought we could die faster sitting in these chairs than we would on the ball field if we kept ourselves in shape by
[Mr. Campbell (Lambton-Kent) .1
playing games. I am sorry to say that that prophecy has been fulfilled. There have been a number of members who have died, and a number of them were younger than I am. I am pleased to be able to say that none of those who participated in the games we have played became casualties. The members to whom I have referred were not athletes. They may have been athletes in their earlier days, but they did not take part in the games we played here. I could cite many other cases to prove the point I have in mind.
For example, I have seen men who could shovel tons of grain, corn and sugar beet on their farms day after day without apparent ill effect. However, after a short time of retirement and a period of idleness they would break down while moving a bit of light, fluffy snow off their sidewalk. They were not fitted to do the work they had previously done.
Now, I feel certain that this legislation could serve a most useful purpose if it were to have the effect of developing a number of good athletes. Then, these athletes could go around the country and tell the people how they became good athletes and how they intend to remain good athletes. The example they set would be an inspiration to the rest of the people. I would stress the point, however, that it is not enough to play games for a while, and on this point I am in disagreement with an hon. member who spoke a while ago and said the playing of games should be limited to those between the ages of 14 and 21 or 22. I stress the fact, as I say, that it is not enough to play games for a while and expect to keep strong and healthy for the rest of your life. It is like your bank balance, you must keep adding to it if you hope to keep spending or you will go broke.
May I venture to say that I have seen many athletes who had trouble in their later years because they trained only for the purpose of excelling at a sport, and for nothing else. When the sport failed to give them a substantial financial return, they neglected themselves and returned to an untrained condition. In this untrained condition they are sometimes tempted to do what they used to be able to do while they were in training. The result is that they have a breakdown in their early years. Apparently, they fail to appreciate the value of maintaining a high standard of physical efficiency or are interested only in the money they receive from the sport. The most important purpose of sport, in the final analysis, is to exemplify the use that can be made of a body that is physically fit. I feel, therefore, there should be those who can speak with authority, who can not only advise people on how to become athletes but also

on how they can retain their athletic ability in the later years of life. May I also stress the fact that those who are less inclined to take part in sports for various reasons, who never try to make the team, are the ones who need the training most and who would benefit from it to a greater degree.
In my opinion, physical fitness comes ahead of athletic prowess. If you are fit, you can become athletic. If you engage in strenuous activities without being fitted for them, you are inviting trouble. I think we witnessed proof of that right on our front lawn here not too many years ago. It is much more important to keep fit in later life than it is to merely learn to play games during one's youth and then neglect oneself later. It is my well considered opinion, based on observation and experience over a period of many years, that the time when there is the greatest need to be physically fit is in the later years of life, when there is a tendency to let down and take things easy. If one has been active in sports in early life, the need becomes even greater than ever for some form of training to be continued in the later years. The medical profession acknowledges that the later years are the dangerous years. I feel very strongly about the fact that any program that is developed should be designed to encourage the people of all ages to engage in sport and thereby benefit from any plan that is approved. In my opinion it is much more important to health to keep fit later in life than merely to learn to play games in the period of youth. By nature the young are generally blessed with the desire to be active. The very young are almost impossible to keep quiet. We older people sometimes need a bit of prodding to get us to do what we know we should do. Our bodies were designed to be worked. I have often stated that it is by work and care of our bodies that we earn and deserve the right to be fit.
At this point I should like to refer to a number of statements that were made by Dr. Thomas K. Cureton, of Urbana, Illinois, a noted authority on physical fitness, while speaking on this subject in London, Ontario, recently. I am quoting from a press report:
-a person can extend his or her active life by 15 to 20 years... by following a moderate program of exercise and relaxation, said Dr. Thomas K. Cureton, of Urbana, Illinois ...
In the United States each year approximately 1,300,000 people have coronary attacks, he said. "They just fold up and it is not due to any disease that can be identified under a microscope. The general state of physical fitness in the United States and Canada is a bit pitiful."
Habits make the difference, he said. Graphs charting the fitness of thousands of people show a pronounced decline at the middle-twenties,-

That is why I stated I do not agree with the remarks of the hon. member who spoke. I should like to repeat this sentence:
Graphs charting the fitness of thousands of people show a pronounced decline at the middle-twenties, when most young people drop active sports for career and household duties.
"Our bodies should be constantly trained to meet the physical and mental stresses that crop up suddenly-"it might be shovelling snow, or severe tension or over-excitement."
He advised all mature individuals to adopt a definite plan of exercise, with these points in mind.
I should also like to refer to the remarks made by the hon. member for Jasper-Edson (Mr. Homer) while speaking in this house on March 16 last as recorded at page 3063 of Hansard. I may say that the hon. member for Jasper-Edson was speaking on the agriculture estimates and was dealing with the use of butter at that particular time. But since he also referred to another matter I am going to quote him here. He states:
-butter is a grade A food which we can eat and enjoy without regard for the bogey man of coronary thrombosis, for behind the threat of coronary thrombosis are a number of other factors besides the cholesterol level in the blood.
I think the greatest underlying factor is a lack of exercise. Canadians and the people of the United States in general are victims of what we might call transportationitis which leads to their taking little physical exercise. This rather than the overeating of fats is probably the greatest cause of heart disease. Of course, I hasten to say that moderation in all things is a sound principle the application of which is essential for good health and this applies to the consumption of animal fats as it applies to other foods.
May I say that I am not one of those who subscribe to the idea that our days are numbered, no matter what we do. I sincerely believe that we can definitely and deliberately add considerably to the length of our own days and, just as definitely, add to the measure of enjoyment of those days, by the way in which we care for our bodies. I believe that we will just as definitely reduce the length of our lives and the measure of enjoyment we get while we live, by taking the opposite course of neglect and misuse. There is a scriptural recording to be found in the 90th psalm, verse 12, which reads as follows:
So teach us to number our days, that we might apply our hearts unto wisdom.
To my mind that is a divine inference that we may number our own days by the way in which we live now. I do not intend the things I have said to seem unkind. In fact, I intend them to be the opposite. While some of the statements may seem to be unkind now, I predict that as the years pass, the day will come when most of those who are listening here and most of those who may read what I have said will agree that the suggestions I have made here are the most

Advisory Council on Sports kindly and most friendly advice that I could have given on this matter. If you lose your health and strength, you have lost everything of value. If you can improve your health and keep it longer, you will have gained the greatest treasure.
I am very pleased to have contributed something to a measure which I am sure can help the people by pointing the way toward that goal whereby they may maintain that sense of well being that will enable them to skip, to run, to jump, to dance, to play, to row a canoe down the Rideau river, to chop a log of firewood, to walk from their home to the parliament buildings or to do almost anything within reason. I suggest that if you keep yourself in condition for these things you can go on year after year doing these things you like to do. I know it can be done by those who are willing to train to that end. I am glad to say something to encourage that training.
These things that I have outlined today, Mr. Speaker, are some of the things that I feel a physical fitness council or representatives of such a council will be obliged to tell the people of our country if they hope to accomplish the greatest measure of success and to make this resolution or this bill serve the purpose it should serve.
May I conclude by saying that I am glad to be able to lend my support to any measure which will inspire the people, young or old, to strive toward that goal whereby they might obtain and maintain that greatest of all possessions, namely health and strength.

Mr. Speaker, in taking part in this debate I should like to associate myself with the hon. members who have preceded me in speaking in their congratulations to the Minister of National Health and Welfare for bringing this resolution before the house. I feel that every member of the house will be in support of this type of resolution. I am sure also that they will join with me in feeling that very beneficial results can follow if this resolution is properly administered. Certainly we all hope that will be the case. The results which can come from legislation such as this are of course, as has been mentioned by previous speakers and as is well known, a healthier nation and a greater national pride. These are probably the two things which are most important in this bill. As I see it, there are two ways in which legislation of this nature can take effect. The first is that it can be forced upon the people. The other- which applies in Canada at least, and I believe it is the only one which should apply -is that this legislation should tend to make sports so attractive that the majority of our people will wish to participate.

The question is asked at the outset, "Why is financial assistance needed in this regard?" I think the first answer is that it is needed to provide the necessary facilities to allow more people to participate in amateur sport and a fitness program. The organization of such a program and the tremendous job of coaching needed is necessarily going to require large sums of money. Travelling expenses for our international representatives, although taken care of normally through other means, should be given consideration in the moneys which are available through this legislation. Then there is the question of the promotion of leadership and incentive to take part in amateur sport. In the promotion of leadership and incentive large sums of money will be required to line up the program across the nation.
I should like at this time to endorse the remarks of the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Smith), who said that the incentive to take part is possibly one of the more important aspects which has to be put across to the people. As far as I am concerned, the incentive to take part is the most important aspect. If a person has not the incentive to take part in a program of this nature, he might as well forget about it.
All of us have had the experience of desiring our children to take part in sports or athletics of some sort. I think that without giving it too much thought many of us from time to time have felt it is essential that our children should do this. To a point it is fairly essential. But as far as team sports are concerned, I have found that a person should be encouraged in the first instance to give it a try. If after giving it a try they find out that they do not desire to continue in that sport, I do not think they should be given any further encouragement, because if they have not the incentive to take part in the sport they will only be a headache to somebody in the future. Therefore in my opinion the incentive to take part is one of the more important aspects of this type of legislation.
This, along with the provision of facilities and the organization of coaching for such a program is going to be one of the main tasks with which the council will have to deal. I believe this can present quite a problem. I think the suggestions put forward in some of the speeches made this afternoon will provide a certain amount of guidance to the council when set up.
There is one other aspect of a program of this nature that is almost as important, if not just as important, as promoting the incentive to take part. I refer to the vast number of volunteer workers throughout Canada who have given freely of their time

for many years in order to promote the incentive for young people to take part in various forms of amateur sport. Without these workers this or any other country would never get very far. These are the people whom it is impossible for any country to replace by paid workers. These are the people who will have to be given a great deal of consideration by the council when it is set up.
When I say they will have to be given a great deal of consideration, I do not mean that consideration should be given in any way, shape or form to paying these people salaries. However, I do feel that money must be spent on encouraging these people who have been doing this work to continue in it. We should encourage more volunteer workers to enter this field. I think the way in which this money can best be spent is in seeing that these people are financially able to attend coaching schools, which schools will undoubtedly have to be set up under this program.
I am sure that every hon. member in the house has come in contact in his own community and others with this vast army of volunteer workers. I am sure we all realize how important they are. However, I should like to dwell on this subject for a moment or two because I believe it is a most important one.
In the town of Flin Flon, Manitoba, in which I live we have been very well blessed with the tremendous number of volunteer workers we have had throughout the years in the field of promoting amateur sport and fitness among the residents of that town. This has resulted in winning a tremendous number of provincial championships for the town. They are too numerous to mention at this time. I believe the number of provincial championships won by teams and individuals representing the town of Flin Flon is a record unsurpassed by any other town in Manitoba.
I am not saying this in a selfish manner of pride in the town of Flin Flon or on behalf of the citizens of the town, but I am trying to make a point in regard to these volunteer workers. Four years ago the junior hockey club of Flin Flon, the Flin Flon Bombers, was successful in winning the memorial cup, emblematic of the junior hockey championship of Canada.
Amateurs?

Yes, definitely amateurs.
Junior hockey in Canada has climbed to a point where most of our major cities only support one club. Some cities, such as Winnipeg, support three or four clubs; but in general even the large eastern cities only support 90205-6-559
Advisory Council on Sports one, and sometimes, two, junior hockey clubs. In fact, most of these cities have on their rosters players imported from all parts of Canada. But when the Flin Flon Bombers won the memorial cup in the spring of 1957, from a town of 15,000 people 11 out of the 15 players on the roster were local boys who had learned and played all their hockey in the town of Flin Flon.
They were playing against a club from the Ottawa-Hull district which had a club with players in it from all over Canada. I must agree that as far as the coaching end of the Flin Flon hockey club is concerned we had a man who is, in my opinion, the top junior coach in Canada and a lot of credit is certainly due to Mr. Bobby Kirk, the coach of that club. However, I do not believe this would ever have been accomplished if it were not for the large number of volunteer workers who gave so freely of their time to managing, coaching, officiating, time keeping etc. and generally taking care of the minor hockey clubs in our town. As I said before, this ap-lies of course to many parts of Canada.
Now I should like to deal with one or two ideas as to how this money could be used to best advantage. First of all, as has been mentioned before, I think the council should give considerable attention to the possibility of conducting nationally sponsored coaching schools in the various provinces of Canada. When I talk about these coaching schools I should like to offer a word of suggestion to the council. I suggest they take a look at the system which the national hockey league has been using for a number of years. The league sends a well known coach and a well known referee to various cities across Canada to conduct one-day clinics in coaching and officiating. This has been beneficial. I think it has shown good results, particularly in western Canada. However, I do not want to see this same system adopted by the council. It is not too bad as far as a one-day school for officials is concerned, because there you have an official of the national hockey league sitting down and discussing the problems which arise in refereeing a hockey game and here you have a teacher instructing people who are going to use this information. But when it comes to a one-day coaching school the situation is entirely different. Here you have a well-known coach attempting to pass on to other people interested in coaching all the fundamentals of coaching a hockey team. He is trying to do all this in one day-to pass on lessons which it has taken him years and years of experience to learn. The difficult part is that he is not only teaching these men how to coach, but that they in turn have to go out and try to impart this information to the

Advisory Council on Sports players. The idea is all right but I do not think that one day is sufficient for a school of this nature. I would therefore suggest that when these coaching schools go across the country serious consideration should be given to extending them over a period of three, four or five days in each area, and for a further period if necessary. I also think the council should consider setting up nationally sponsored schools in most regions of Canada for volunteer workers, not only to impart to them the idea that Canada in general appreciates their services but to impart ways and means of adding to their value in this field.
I think, also, that schools should be conducted for organizers in the various parts of Canada. Some people may say we are going to have too many schools. However, these are three entirely different fields of endeavour; one is for coaching, the other is for volunteer workers and the other is for organizers. I feel it is essential we should have these organizers, particularly if any form of recreation in addition to strictly amateur sport and fitness is to be taken into consideration.
A few years ago, when legislation similar to this was in being, the province of Manitoba was among the provinces which took advantage of the federal legislation to the extent that it assisted communities which had decided to employ a recreation director. The provincial authority paid part of the cost incurred by the communities concerned. The result was good in many cases, but in some cases the municipalities were merely engaging these men because federal aid was available. Their programs fell through, and eventually the legislation was taken off the statute books in Ottawa and discontinued. I think the council which will he set up under the terms of this legislation should give consideration to assisting, through the provincial authorities, any communities which are interested in paying their share of acquiring a recreation director.
The legislation with which we are dealing is certainly very controversial, and many of us have our own ideas of how it should be worked out. In 1958 there was a Canadian Press ballot asking the following question: "Should the federal government subsidize amateur sport in an effort to develop athletes of international calibre for a healthier nation?" The voting at that time was 86 in favour and 20 against. Hon. members will see, therefore, that this, is a very controversial question. However, I am sure every one of us here is anxious to see this bill come into force and to play his part in seeing that it works.
There are many who feel that all forms of recreation should come under this bill. I know

that a large number of the people in the town in which I live feel this way. However, for the time being I think the council should take its first look at assisting fitness and amateur sport. As time goes on, possibly the other forms of recreation could be included. If that were to come about I think more money would be needed. However, I believe that could wait for a year or two yet.
I believe, also, that when we talk of sponsored coaches and organizers the council should give consideration to hiring coaches and organizers on a full time basis in some specific cases. But they must be men of proven ability. There have been times in the past when Canada has lost valuable coaches through the lack of employment opportunities in this field in Canada. I think they should be careful about this and that consideration should not be given to everyone who may call himself a coach. Only coaches of proven ability should be given this consideration.
I think we must examine means of making better use of our existing facilities to achieve greater results in this field. When we examine the question of assisting our teams to participate in the field of international sports we should consider the possibility of using the facilities of the Royal Canadian Air Force as a means of transporting our players. The planes of the R.C.A.F. make trips during the week to many countries in the world and perhaps these facilities could be used by our athletes representing Canada in international sports events.
Greater use should also be made of the facilities of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to publicize important sports events and our outstanding athletes. Many people have said that the radio has made the national hockey league the financial success it is. This applies not only to Toronto but other areas. I agree that radio broadcasts have tended to increase the gates in various cities and I feel that the C.B.C. through its television facilities could render a valuable service to amateur sports in Canada by giving them publicity. If more publicity were given to our national athletes through television and other means an additional incentive would be created for more people to participate in sports events.
I do not recall having seen televised a single national amateur hockey final. Professional hockey games are televised consistently and often the national league finals are not sponsored but are presented as a public service of the C.B.C. The same should be done with respect to amateur finals.
Each of us must ask himself this question: How do I feel about Canada's prestige in the matter of international sports events such as

the Olympic games? As legislators we must answer this question. The sports council, of course, must also face this question and answer it. We talk glibly about our prestige and national pride in athletics, but what do we actually do about it? I have advanced a few suggestions which I feel are deserving of consideration. I wish particularly to stress the importance of achieving greater publicity through the facilities of the C.B.C. I ask hon. members to consider how well they remember the athletes who through a great deal of self denial have brought honours to Canada by winning Olympic gold medals. Most of us recall, of course, how thrilled we were as a nation when Percy Williams astounded all the experts by bringing two gold medals to Canada in 1928 when he won both the 100 metre and the 200 metre dash. This was the second time that Canada had won a sprint. I wonder how many hon. members will recall who brought that honour to Canada on a previous occasion? In 1908 Mr. R. Kerr won the 200 metre event in the Olympics.
We remember people such as Percy Williams simply because of the publicity which was given at the time of the event. Probably none of us has given a second thought to the fact that in 1928 when Percy Williams returned from the Olympic games with two gold medals Ethel Catherwood of Saskatoon also brought home a gold medal for winning the ladies' running high jump. I recall this because on her return a public reception was held in her honour at Winnipeg.
We all remember Barbara Ann Scott who in 1948 won the ladies' figure skating event but we remember her mainly because of the publicity that was accorded her success. How many of us remember Canada's only gold medalist in individual events in 1952? Honours were won in that year by young George Genereux of Saskatoon in the trap shooting event. Back in 1908 the same honour was brought to Canada when the gold medal was won by W. H. Ewing. I wonder how many of us remember the names Robert Paul and Barbara Wagner who won the figure skating pairs medal this year at Squaw Valley? Probably in a year or two their names will have been forgotten by many of us. We do not forget the names of people like Jesse Owens and other United States winners because of the tremendous publicity accorded them. Their names are by-words when we come to think of athletics. We tend to forget the names of our Canadian athletes and yet as a nation we sometimes feel very deflated when our athletes fail to measure up to the standards of the athletes of other nations.
Some hon. members have suggested that we must be careful not to allow this money to be spent in such a way that professionals 90205-6-559J
Advisory Council on Sports will receive the final benefits and with this I agree. I am heartily in accord with the statement made by the hon. member for Calgary South who said that professional sport certainly has its place in our way of life. Professional sport serves as an incentive to many young people to participate in amateur games, an incentive which we as legislators and citizens have probably failed to give them.
Before closing 1 wish to draw to the attention of hon. members the record of Canadian athletes in Olympic games in the past. Of how many of these outstanding athletes have we even heard? The marathon was won only once, by Mr. W. J. Sherring in 1906. The
10.000	metre walk was won only once, by Mr. G. H. Goulding, in 1912. The 110 metre hurdle was won only once, by Mr. E. J. Thomson in 1920. The men's running high jump was won once in 1932. This event was given a little publicity so probably many of us remember Dune MacNaughton. The sled dog racing event was won once, in 1932 by Emil St. Godard of The Pas, Manitoba.
Turning now to hockey it will be remembered that Canada won the event in 1920, 1924, 1928 and 1932. It was not until 1936 that for the first time Canada did not win. That was the year that Great Britain, with a team composed mostly of players who learned their hockey in Canada, won the Olympic hockey event. In 1948 and 1952 Canada won but in 1956 the U.S.S.R. won and in 1960 the event was won by the United States.
As I said, there are some who say that we must make sure that this money is not spent so that the professional people will derive the ultimate benefit. When some of them say that, I think that possibly they have in mind the hockey situation in Canada today. I think that amateur hockey in Canada should be given all the support that the council can give it because the Canadian amateur hockey association, one of the largest sport groups in Canada, with a registration of approximately
120.000	players from the lowest age group up, has only one paid official, their secretary-manager, Mr. Gordon Juckes of Melville, Saskatchewan. They have only one paid official in their whole organization which looks after the interests of 120,000 children. When you compare Canada's hockey record with its record in other sports in Olympic competition, I think it is obvious that this is one sport that should be given every encouragement by the committee so that our prestige in Olympic competition with respect to our national game can be restored and maintained in the future in order that Canada may come out on top in Olympic competition in this event as we did in the past.

Advisory Council on Sports In the 1960 summer Olympic games Canada finished twenty sixth out of 53 countries competing and in the winter Olympics at Squaw Valley Canada finished eighth out of 16. When our children come home from school with their report cards and have marks under 50 we feel that something is wrong and something must be done about the situation. If we look at our record in the 1960 Olympics we find that in the winter games we did get 50 per cent but in the summer Olympics we were slightly below that mark. So far as the field of international sport is concerned, I would say that the council to be set up should take into consideration all factors which will assist Canada to produce athletes who can compare favourably with the athletes of other countries. It is not always absolutely necessary that they win. As long as they go to these games and give a good account of themselves, we are all proud of them. However, I believe that the council should give the fullest consideration to those athletes who will be competing in international sport. I should like to suggest particularly that the council should not be scared away from hockey because of the fact that the professionals eventually get most of our hockey players. I think the council should take a look at our great record in hockey in the past and give it as much support as any other branch of amateur sport in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, at this time I should also like to extend my congratulations to the minister for bringing in this legislation. I believe it is good legislation and I certainly support the contention of previous speakers this afternoon. I do not believe we can minimize the importance of sport in its various phases from amateur right through to professional. A great deal has been said this afternoon about those who have excelled in various sports in the past. I should like to ask the question, what about those who do not excel? What about the average hockey player, the average basketball player, the average tennis player or the average player in any kind of sport? I think these are the people whom we should assist.
At the present time there are established councils all across Canada. There are a great number in small communities as well as a great number in the larger centres. I think these are the people who need assistance. I should like to suggest to the minister that we use our existing government agencies. In most districts across Canada there are already recreational directors who have been appointed by a province or municipality or perhaps by a county. I believe we should use the present administrative set-up rather than establishing elaborate administrative machinery at this time. I believe we should

work with the municipal authorities who are in possession of the facts as to local needs and the necessity of promoting sport among the younger generation.
I was very pleased to see that the word "recreation" has been omitted from the bill. Otherwise we would have been in the impossible position of possibly supplying coaches for ardent bridge players or golfers and we might even have found ourselves in the position of supplying coaches for those who play tiddly-winks. I believe that we should cut down the overhead and see that financial help is given to the smaller groups rather than spending tremendous amounts on administration and for council meetings, joint meetings and other meetings all over Canada.
There is another point I should like to bring to the minister's attention. We must cover all types of sport. Various organizations have made pleas. I received one this afternoon from the Canadian amateur hockey association. I believe we should also give consideration to the Canadian amateur basketball association, the Canadian amateur football association, the Canadian amateur rugby association and so on so that we will cover all kinds of sport.
I should also like to have the assurance that the $5 million will be spent for the benefit of those in need of physical fitness, and I believe that in initiating this program we have to start with the youth of the country. Thousands of our younger generation are looking for leadership at the present time and I know that the minister and the government are capable of and willing to give such leadership.
A great deal has been said this afternoon about the necessity of training coaches. I should like to take a slightly different view. I believe coaches are a necessity but what might happen is that we might train a great number of coaches who would be allocated to the larger centres in Canada. I believe that the situation is just as serious in our smaller municipal centres where it would be impossible to obtain people qualified to teach amateur sports to a small group. Elimination of the smaller centres in Canada would have a serious effect. If we look at the line-ups of teams that have excelled in different sports we will find that the majority of the players have come from small communities.
At this point I should like to take hon. members back a few years to 1936 or 1937. In British Columbia at that time there was formed what was called a "pro-rec" department. The provincial government of the day spent thousands of dollars on this program which in my view was a very good one if

it had been properly organized and administered. In my own little area, we received over $2,000 worth of physical education equipment, and yet today I do not believe that any part of this equipment can be located. I feel we have a tremendous job to do in supplying leadership for this program.
In addition, I should like to suggest that we should support those who are working with our younger people in all lines of sports. They will produce better hockey players, better baseball players, better basketball players, better lacrosse players, across Canada. There are a great number of these sports that have been played on small playing fields or small sheets of ice, without the use of the elaborate buildings that have been suggested from time to time in this debate. I cannot help, Mr. Speaker, but pass along a word of congratulation to all those voluteer workers to which the previous speaker referred, who are the backbone of our amateur sports in Canada. It is on the basis of their work that we are going to establish this physical fitness and make it possible for our young people in Canada to reach that goal towards which they have been striving for a number of years.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the minister upon the introduction of this bill. I think it is an excellent one and one which is long overdue. I believe it will be one that will provide a broad basis upon which governments, federal, provincial and municipal, will be able to build. We should keep in mind, at the same time, all the pitfalls that are related to the problems of coaching, classes and the even distribution of funds across Canada.
It is no secret that young Canadians have not participated in sports and training to the extent that they should. This participation in training has become necessary over the years in the light of changing conditions in Canada. In 1900 over 50 per cent of the population was engaged in working on farms, doing physical work from daylight to dark. Today, only 10 per cent of the people work on farms because these farms have become mechanized and most of the heavy work is done by machinery. The greater part of our population today is living in urban areas. Even here, the physical work is being cut to a minimum through the use of power mowers, power shovels and snow ploughs. All these things have reduced the physical work tremendously. Shorter working hours have provided a great deal of leisure time. As a matter of fact, not long ago I saw a statement by a psychologist to the effect that the ideal day consists of eight hours work, eight hours sleep, and eight hours play. I believe it is the eight hours of playtime that must be better planned. People
Advisory Council on Sports require physical work to keep their muscles, heart and other organs functioning properly. People require physical work not only to keep these organs fit but also in order to eliminate waste products in the bloodstream and to burn up other by-products which may be deposited in the body and do irreparable harm.
It is a fact that most Canadians follow occupations which are classed as sedentary. Most of us overeat and do not take sufficient exercise, if we take any at all. Any contribution that this bill will make towards interesting the people of Canada in proper exercise and physical fitness, will contribute in no small measure to the happiness of the individual and to his feeling of well being. In addition, it will also add a few years of extra life. The interest aroused in physical fitness and regular exercise will result in improving the mental condition of our people. I am thinking particularly of the stresses and strains of modern life which drive people to seek tranquillizers and sleeping pills. A physically tired body is a healthy body and of itself encourages relaxation and sleep.
I think, too, of our teenagers and young people with all the spare time that they have on their hands. The other day I noticed that a religionist pointed out that the spare time we have today is one of the tragedies of our time; that the responsibility of charting the activities in which young people engage must be faced by all of us. The fashion for the young people is to get a car of some vintage or other and go places. Most of the appeal is from commercial establishments trying to make a dollar from these people. Some of these teenagers join gangs. An outlet must be found for all this youthful exuberance, and it is small wonder that it finds an outlet in fights and so forth. An interest in sport is inherent in most youngsters, therefore we do have a great responsibility in providing opportunities for planned sport, physical fitness classes and general activities which require physical work. None of our youth in Canada must be by-passed. We must give the youth of this country an opportunity to try to mobilize to become physically and morally strong people with the spiritual courage to make Canada a model for the world to copy.

Mr. Speaker, I deem it a privilege to rise and speak briefly on this bill to encourage physical fitness and amateur sport. I do not intend to go into the broad principles of the bill which have been well covered by the many speakers who have preceded me. However, sir, there is one sport to which I should like to refer and there is one part of the bill about which I should like to speak briefly. I do not want anyone
8862	HOUSE OF
Advisory Council on Sports to think I am partial to a particular sport. However, we have heard references to hockey, lacrosse, baseball, football and a great variety of sports. I should like to bring to the attention of the minister amateur rowing.
Now, amateur rowing is a sport in which many municipalities cannot participate because it is a water sport. However, it is a sport in which the participants must attain a very high standard of physical fitness. They must spend many long hours in training, and often with very little publicity. This particular sport, amateur rowing, is well supported by our universities and colleges, and in many cases by our public and high schools. It is a sport, therefore, that we must keep to the forefront; we must not allow it to die out. It is a sport that requires very expensive equipment, but there seem to be those throughout the country who are prepared to help supply it. I think the minister should also lend his support. Many Canadians who in the past have followed this sport have gone abroad and in competition with oarsmen from other countries have brought to Canada national fame through winning what is known as the Diamond Sculls which is the world championship for rowing. I can recall at the present time four who brought that honour to Canada.
In the riding which I have the honour to represent we have a very active rowing club which is fully supported by the high schools. We also have the Henley course which is the course to which students from many high schools in the province of Ontario and in other parts of Canada come from time to time during the summer to hold their contests. At the Henley course there we also have once a year the big event, when teams from the United States and all over Canada come to contest for the international championship.
Rowing is probably not the most important sport in Canada but nevertheless it is an important sport in Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and Germany, and more particularly in Great Britain. It is a sport that develops strength of character. It is truly a builder of physical fitness and young manhood. When the Minister of National Health and Welfare is considering the setting up of the physical fitness council, which is part of the bill, I would ask that he give consideration to having on that council someone who is an authority on amateur rowing, as I feel that rowing is a very important sport for our universities, our colleges and our high schools.
I am not going to deal any further with the bill. I realize that many have spoken. I


concur in most of what has been said and I wish to lend my support one hundred per cent to the bill itself.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to assure you at the outset that I shall be very brief in the remarks I have to make regarding this very outstanding piece of legislation which the minister has brought before us. I think all phases have been covered very thoroughly. However, I should like to bring to the attention of the minister and the council that he shall appoint the fact that, to the best of my knowledge, nowhere in Canada is there a university that provides a degree in the faculty of physical education. I believe that anyone in Canada who wishes to specialize in this field must go to the United States in order to obtain such a degree. I would think that Canada has arrived at the point, having regard to her population and her stature, that we should have in Canada a university that would provide such a degree in physical education.
At this time, if I may, Mr. Speaker, I should like to suggest that the University of Toronto, at their faculty of agriculture situated in Guelph, has one of the finest physical education buildings to be found anywhere in North America. It would lend itself ideally to the formation of a faculty of physical education for Canada.
I should like to say how much I as a member appreciate-as I am sure do all other hon. members-the great work the volunteer coaches are doing in the field of amateur sport throughout Canada. I am sure this legislation will serve a very useful purpose in bringing about fitness and improving amateur sport throughout Canada. In so doing we shall be developing young Canadians who will be the citizens of tomorrow.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder if I could interrupt our proceedings at this stage to ask for consent to revert to motions in order to deal with a matter pertaining to the divorce bills on the order paper.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Has the hon. member leave to revert to motions?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The house has before it a number of divorce bills which could perhaps be dealt with promptly within the next two days if we take certain action now.
This has been a difficult problem for parliament to resolve, that is, the method of dealing with divorce bills, and over the last two years a great deal of time has been spent in attempting to reach a solution. On some occasions we seem to have come very close to doing so, but not with the unanimity that is desirable. However, in view of the fact that the people who have made application for divorces have done so bona fide as far as we know and have complied with the law of the land it might seem wise to the house to deal with these bills this year and to continue to search for what some people consider would be a better solution to this entire problem. I am prepared to make this statement for the record which, if agreed to by other parties in the house, might permit us to proceed with the divorce bills on this occasion. I should like to make this statement: the question of procedure with respect to parliamentary divorce is under study, and the government has hopes of being able to present to the house at the next session some proposals in this regard.
If that is acceptable to the house then perhaps at this stage we might at least agree later on tonight or when we have completed our discussion on the Pine Point railway bill-if we do complete it-or certainly before the house rises at 10.30 to give second reading to the divorce bills on the order paper. These would then go to the standing committee on miscellaneous private bills for consideration tomorrow and when they
Private Bills
return from that committee they will be available to the house for third reading.

I think that what the leader of the house has said will commend itself to my friends in the house. As is well known there are a number of hon. members on both sides who would, perhaps, not wish to approve these bills but I think there is a feeling that, as long as this procedure and no other exists, persons who have acted in good faith should not be denied a relief which has been available since confederation.
Indeed, I would hazard the suggestion that rather than embark during the next ten minutes on the affairs of the Pine Point railway and then go back to the other bill and return to the Pine Point railway matter again before considering this subject further, that if there were no objection from any other quarter of the house we might during the next ten minutes carry out the suggestion made by the leader of the house and give second reading to these bills which are on the order paper and send them to the committee right away in order that they might be considered as soon as possible.

If a solution to this particularly vexing parliamentary problem could have been found and agreed upon earlier this session it might, at least, have contributed to a less apoplectic attitude on the part of some hon. members who are not with us at the moment.
However, as far as the researches of the government and others are concerned, we look forward with great hopes and anticipation to a solution of this problem. We hope that at the next session this difficulty may be overcome as far as parliament is concerned and that these particular bills will be able to be dealt with in a more expeditious, fairer and more just manner.
With regard to the bills now before us I think it would take not the ten minutes we have until six o'clock to give them second reading. If past practice is followed of passing them by automation I am sure we could give them passage within 10 or 15 seconds.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
One other waiver of the formalities of the rules is necessary to permit the committee to sit at once and I take it the intention of the house following the statement

of the Minister of Veterans Affairs is that the committee proceed to consider these bills and report on them, if it can, so that they may come back to the house without undue delay.
I draw the attention of hon. members to the wording of paragraph 1 of standing order No. 106:
106 (1) No committee on any private bill originating in this house is to consider the same until after one week's notice of the sitting of such committee has been first affixed in the lobby; nor, in the case of any such bill originating in the Senate, until after 24 hours' like notice.
Therefore, it will be seen that 24 hours' notice would be required. If the house would give consent to the suspension of the standing order with respect to these particular bills which have just received second reading it would be possible for the committee to proceed.

There are some bills which might be considered contentious concerning which there is some likelihood of contestation arising out of irregularities which might exist. By the waiving of this rule we would not wish to deprive individuals the right of a hearing of their case nor to have dissolution of marriage granted when perhaps it should not be granted.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member will be prepared to leave that to the good sense and judgment of the committee. It is a matter for them. This waiver would only permit the bills to come before the committee. On that basis, is it agreed?
Agreed.

Mr. Speaker, before the next order is called, may I suggest to the house leader that we call it six o'clock now. It seems rather absurd to embark on a discussion of the Pine Point railway bill for five minutes and then to come back to the other bill which was not fully completed. In making this suggestion perhaps I should ask the house leader if it is clearly understood that we will be disposing of the other bill at 7.30 so that no hon. member will feel, if he is a few minutes late, that he is being restricted in his rights.

Advisory Council on Sports

maintopic: ESTABLISHMENT OP ADVISORY COUNCIL ON PHYSICAL FITNESS AND AMATEUR SPORT

speechtext:
The house resumed consideration in committee of Bill No. C-131, to encourage fitness and amateur sport-Mr. Monteith (Perth)- Mr. Chown in the chair.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 7.30 p.m.
On clause 7-Council established. (Translation):

maintopic: ESTABLISHMENT OP ADVISORY COUNCIL ON PHYSICAL FITNESS AND AMATEUR SPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, following the brief discussion we had this afternoon with respect to the French version of the bill now before the committee, I should like to propose this amendment to subsection (4) of section 7:
That Bill C-131 be amended by the deletion of subsection (4) of section 7, and its replacement by the following, in the French version:
(4) Au sein du Conseil, chaque province doit compter au moins un membre qui en provient.
Now, with regard to the other point raised by my hon. friend from St. Denis (Mr. Denis) concerning the translation of the word "fitness", I must say, first of all, that the translators have looked into this problem, and this may seem peculiar to the hon. members, but the word "fitness" is extremely difficult to translate in the present context. Personally, I think that the word "sante" was well suited for the definition of the bill, because this is an act to promote health through amateur sport. After all, a person who does not enjoy good health can regain health through sports and athletics.
However, if the committee insists on having the word "sante" replaced because it is a little too vague or because it could lead to confusion, I should tell the committee that it has been suggested to me that in such a case, the expression "condition de l'individu" could be substituted for the word "sante". The title would then read as follows: "Favorisant la condition de l'individu par la pratique du sport amateur". Then the word "sante" would be replaced by the expression "condition de l'individu" wherever it appears in the bill.

maintopic: ESTABLISHMENT OP ADVISORY COUNCIL ON PHYSICAL FITNESS AND AMATEUR SPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I hope you will forgive me for interrupting the minister but the word "condition" means nothing in itself. The words "condition physique" or "sante physique" would be all right.
During the recess hour, we ventured to consult the larger dictionaries. We found that, the word "fitness" was translated by "sante
physique". It may seem strange, but the translation of fitness is "sant6 physique". Everyone knows that we usually say: "He is in good condition; he is in form". However, "sant6 physique" is defined in the dictionary by the words "en forme". By itself, the word "sante" would have no meaning, just like "condition" used alone would have no meaning.
I therefore suggest that we simply add to the word "sante" the adjective "physique".

maintopic: ESTABLISHMENT OP ADVISORY COUNCIL ON PHYSICAL FITNESS AND AMATEUR SPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think that what my colleague the Minister of National Health and Welfare wanted to make clear is that we are concerned here with both mental and physical health. Besides, the well known saying ''mens sana in corpore sano" shows that the word "sante" is used for both mental health and physical health.
When my colleague the Minister of National Health and Welfare suggested that we use that word in the French version, he meant that this legislation encourages physical and mental health of the individual.
As regards the word "condition", that word has an athletic meaning. Here is the definition I find in the Larousse dictionary:
Is applied to animals and athletes whose physical fitness has reached the highest degree of development. when they are capable of putting forth without fatigue the effort for which they are trained.
So we do not need the words "bonne condition" when speaking of the "condition de 1'individu", because it would be a pleonasm. In this case, it should be "condition".
As for me, I am far from being a linguist, but I am of the opinion that the word "sante" is a good translation of "fitness", since it means in fact the physical and intellectual or mental health of the individual.

maintopic: ESTABLISHMENT OP ADVISORY COUNCIL ON PHYSICAL FITNESS AND AMATEUR SPORT
speechtext: If it is a case of explaining the intention of the Minister of Health and Welfare when he talks about "physical and mental health', why not amend the English version by substituting the word "health" to the word "fitness". The English version can be amended as well as the French. I do not see why we should always try to amend the French version when the English can be amended when the meaning, is not the same. Besides, the hon. member who just spoke knows very well that when we talk about a man in good health, we mean a man who is not sick in bed, who does not suffer from arthritis, who has no heart condition; that is what is meant by health.

maintopic: ESTABLISHMENT OP ADVISORY COUNCIL ON PHYSICAL FITNESS AND AMATEUR SPORT
speechtext: He does not suffer from rheumatism.

maintopic: ESTABLISHMENT OP ADVISORY COUNCIL ON PHYSICAL FITNESS AND AMATEUR SPORT
speechtext:
"Fitness" simply means that a man is in good physical condition. But if the

Advisory Council on Sports Minister of National Health and Welfare has something else in mind and wants mental health to be included as well as physical fitness, he can express it as well in English as in French. Therefore, let him translate the French word "sante" by "health" in the English version. What is sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander.
(Text):

maintopic: ESTABLISHMENT OP ADVISORY COUNCIL ON PHYSICAL FITNESS AND AMATEUR SPORT
speechtext: I think there is a great deal in what the hon. member for St. Denis has just said. I say there is some doubt as to just what the word "fitness" means. Surely, the whole problem would be solved if we changed the English title to "an act to encourage physical fitness". There would be no question about translating that by "sante physique". We all remember the old jokes by Stephen Leacock on the word "fitness". He asked, fitness for what? Fitness was, of course, really a slang expression up until a generation ago and it is only recently that it has become an accepted English word. I do think that perhaps we might resolve this difficulty if we were to put the adjective in both titles and it would make it clearer that we are not attempting to invade the realm of the spirit, which is perhaps within the provincial jurisdiction, if we can judge by some of the resolutions-

maintopic: ESTABLISHMENT OP ADVISORY COUNCIL ON PHYSICAL FITNESS AND AMATEUR SPORT
speechtext: Are you opposed to mental fitness?

maintopic: ESTABLISHMENT OP ADVISORY COUNCIL ON PHYSICAL FITNESS AND AMATEUR SPORT
speechtext:
No, I am not opposed to mental fitness. I think even this house could profit from it. I do not know whether, in view of the fact that although the government promised this before the last election, the Minister of National Health and Welfare has never been willing to pay the federal share of the cost of people in mental hospitals, can be taken as an indication that they regard mental fitness as a provincial matter.

as well as the physical well-being of the participants. speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider Bill No. C-126, respecting the construction of a line of railway in the province of Alberta and in the Northwest Territories by Canadian National Railway Company from a point at or near Grimshaw, in the province of Alberta, in a northerly direction to Great Slave lake, in the Northwest Territories.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman. Actually there was quite an extended discussion of this project at the resolution stage and then on second reading. subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE

Canadian National Railways
