subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext:
Once again I want to remind the committee and the hon. member for Laurier that this is the first time an agreement of this type has ever been put in the hands of the committee at this stage. These agreements have always been kept confidential. It is the first time that the government has ever placed such an agreement in the hands of the committee. The hon. member says that the agreement is not signed. I never said the agreement was signed. I said that

in relation to this agreement I have received a letter from Pine Point Mines Limited, from Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company and from the C.N.R. stating that they are ready to sign such agreement if the bill is approved by the house. This is the situation at the present time. There is no mystery about that; there is no secrecy. It is an open book. This agreement was placed in the hands of every hon. member of the committee. The hon. member for Laurier had time to read it twice.
As I said before the standing committee, the Department of Justice is still reviewing the agreement to check whether there are any legal errors in it, or anything of that kind, which should be corrected. At that time I also invited hon. members of the committee to make suggestions on this agreement. However, I must remind the committee that this agreement is actually requested in clause 6 of the bill, which makes it a condition. The government is ready to build a railway. We set forth in clause 6 some very clear conditions that have to be met by Pine Point Mines, Cominco and the C.N.R. before the bill before the committee comes into force and before the railway is built.
The hon. member also asked how this railway is going to be financed. I have stated, and he has recognized, that as far as the operation and the maintenance of the railway is concerned, the C.N.R. has a guarantee that what is going to be paid by the company for the moving of its concentrates will meet the maintenance and the operation of this line. Also, the company is giving a guarantee of 215,000 tons of traffic for 10 years. This will cover the operation and the maintenance of the line.
Therefore this railway will not be a source of deficit for the C.N.R. It will become an integral part of the C.N.R. and in addition, Canadian National Railways will have this great advantage of being the sole mover of these concentrates on the run between Edmonton and Calgary and will share half and half from Grimshaw to Edmonton on the Northern Alberta Railways, which is jointly owned by the C.N.R. and C.P.R.
As far as the financing of the capital for the building of this line is concerned, this is going to be paid out of an item in the estimates of the Department of Transport. These estimates come before the committee every year. Part of the capital will be reimbursed out of payments that are mentioned in schedule B of the agreement and also in subclause (a) of clause 6. These payments to Her Majesty can reach $20 million. This is part of the cost on the part of Pine Point Mines as its share in the building of this great undertaking of a railway in the north.

Of course, we could have built that railroad simply for the development of the north. It is a rather long railway; it is a huge railway, but we have such confidence in the north of Canada, with all its mineral richness and also, in that particular area, the tremendous reserves of timber and agricultural products, that I think the government would have been justified in building the railway. However, we are fortunate enough that there are proven reserves of lead and zinc which are ready to be developed, which development is going to be undertaken by Pine Point Mines, a subsidiary of Cominco. I think we got a very good deal from this new mine both for the government and for Canadian National Railways, and I recommend it to the committee.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE

Mr. Chairman, the minister has not dealt with the question which I put to him. He did give the method and the manner in which the Department of Transport will handle this money, by setting aside an estimate. But my question to the minister was this: what will the taxpayer get for the maximum amount of $86 million that is being invested by the government? I think the committee is entitled to know that.
Then, what provision is being made for servicing that capital? What provision is being made for interest during construction, because this railway will not be completed until 1966? Therefore as the railway is constructed large sums of money will have to be provided. Whether it will be $25 million at the end of the first year and $20 million at the end of the second year and so on, I do not know; but the government does not manufacture that money. The government will have to borrow it and will have to pay interest on it.
I think the committee is entitled to know, (1) what will the taxpayer get for this capital amount of money that is being invested in the line? Then (2), what provision is being made for servicing the capital; and (3), what provision is being made for the interest during construction?

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member asks, what is the taxpayer going to get for this investment? First of all, this is going to be a brand new railway which will become an integral part of the C.N.R., and as such any profit on that line will serve to reduce the deficit of the C.N.R., which is a crown-owned agency and for which the taxpayers of Canada have to put up the money to cover the deficit each year.
With regard to how the money will be paid, I think clause 5 is quite clear. It says:
The subsidy hereby authorized shall be paid to the company out of the consolidated revenue fund by the payment from time to time, at the
Canadian National Railways direction of the governor in council upon the report of the Minister of Transport as to the mileage of railway line constructed or to be constructed, of such amounts, in such manner and subject to such conditions, if any, as the governor in council deems expedient.
I think it is quite clear here that the governor in council will decide in what manner and subject to what conditions these payments will be made, how the debt will be serviced and how the interest will be met. It will be all done by order in council, as is set forth in clause 5.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext: Then from what the minister has said, am I right in assuming that all the taxpayer can expect to get back is the amount mentioned in clause 6(a), namely, a maximum of $20 million.

speechtext: I did not hear an answer from the minister to the last question asked by the hon. member for Laurier. I saw him nod his head.

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Laurier asked a question. It was not a question seeking specific information lying exclusively within the knowledge of the Minister of Transport. It was a question which, I think, any member of this house with a little reasonable understanding of what is involved should be able to answer, and I propose to answer it.
The question was: what does the taxpayer get. It seems to me the grand old man of the Liberal party Sir Wilfrid Laurier who said "the twentieth century belongs to Canada" would turn in his grave if he heard these trifling and petulant quibblings on a question of this kind. Here is a railway which is going to open up a brand new empire and before we get through I propose to submit very briefly, perhaps later on in the proceedings, some of the statements which appear in the record of the Manning royal commission concerning the assets of the area which will be contributing to this line of railway. As a matter of fact, I think this will probably be one of the last great railways ever built on this continent.
The taxpayer is going to get (a) a line of railway built to the Pine Point mine which is at this time of sufficient importance to justify the company in spending a total of almost $40 million at Pine Point itself and at Trail, in addition to the large and substantial sums which will be contributed by the others concerned. The taxpayer will receive (b) the benefits which will naturally arise from the bringing into production of an area lying from 40 miles north of Grimshaw to Hay River with
8878	HOUSE OF
Canadian National Railways tremendous resources in agriculture, timber, fishing, natural gas and petroleum. This is not a speculative proposition. These things have been, to some extent, found, and they have been the subject already of some development. They have waited for one thing only -the construction of this railway. The province of Alberta has stated that it will not open up new townships or land in this particular area unless and until some provision for transportation is made. This was the statement made to the Manning royal commission on behalf of the Alberta government, and the same statement has been made to me by officials of that government charged with the responsibility of the settlement of this area. When this railroad is built, and as it progresses, there is no doubt that thousands of new townships will be established and land opened up for cultivation. The same applies to timber. Surely, any national development on this scale which brings into production resources of this order is bound to have the effect of reducing the capital cost of this railway.
Evidence was given before the standing committee about which the hon. gentleman spoke that both the railway company and the mining company had made certain calculations as a result of which they felt that the rates which are to be charged, and which are referred to in the schedules to the agreement, should be sufficient to repay the operating and maintenance charges of the railway. Anything else above that is bound to result in a reduction of the capital sum. If some hon. members want it put in dollars and cents, that is what the taxpayer is getting. What is of far more importance are the benefits which will derive from the opening up of this region. Moreover, when this railroad gets to the south shore of Great Slave lake it will make available at substantially reduced prices, goods, commodities and services whose cost, up to the present time, has been at a substantial level. This high cost of goods and services have had the effect of holding back to some extent the expansion of development in the mining area in the Northwest Territories. The minute this railway gets to the port of Hay River hon. members will see an acceleration in the rate of development which will, I think, be of tremendous benefit of the whole country. These are not pipe dreams. I have been up there and talked with these people.
I think that is a fair answer to the hon. member for Laurier. He asked a valid question and I have, I think, given him a reasonable answer.

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE

Perhaps I might say just a word in connection with what the hon. member for Peace River has said. He has


attempted to give an answer covering what is generally done in connection with a developmental railway. We all know what the practice is in connection with such railways. I simply say that there are on the record three questions to which I have not received satisfactory answers.
I go on, now to another question. It was stated in the committee that the title to this line would be with the Canadian National Railways although the government would pay for it. My question is: what is being done by the government to protect its interest of between $75 million and $86 million less the subsidy paid by the Pine Point Company, with the C.N.R. in reference to its investment? Here is a sum of between $75 million and $86 million which is to be put into the construction of this line. subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext: As I said earlier, the government is building the railroad from Grimshaw to Pine Point. The railway is going to become part of the C.N.R. system. It is going to be operated by the Canadian National Railways and it is going to be built by the railway company; it will become, also, the property of the C.N.R. As far as the government is concerned there will be, first of all, this $20 million capital payment by the users of this line. In addition, the taxpayers will get as a return for their contribution a reduction in the C.N.R. deficit. There will be a net contribution to the C.N.R. system, and that contribution will provide for the carrying charges on the capital investment. As I said, this line will become part of the Canadian National Railways system which is a government-owned corporation and as such it will still be the property of the Canadian public and the Canadian taxpayers.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the C.N.R. provides a service for the government, the government pays for that service. The estimates of the Department of Transport are replete with items for subsidies representing services which the C.N.R. provides to the government and the people of Canada. government has provided no protection but has simply said that if there is a surplus it will be used to reduce the deficit of the C.N.R.

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext: At what time?

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext: Did the C.N.R. make a study of the economics of this project and then recommend it to the government?

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman. That is all a matter of history. subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext: The minister has not replied to my question, so I shall restate it. Did the government make a study of the economics of the project or did the C.N.R. make one? That is what I wish to know.

speechtext: Both did. I mean the government made a study before proposing this measure to the house. subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext:
At both the resolution and second reading stages, hon. members of this group supported this measure in principle. Mr. Chairman, I have heard the question posed a couple of times as to what the people are going to get for the $86 million that is going to be invested in this railway. The first thing that comes to my mind is that they are going to get a railway that was promised them by the Liberal party 30 years ago but which the Liberals never quite got around to building. That is the first thing that I can see they are going to get.
From some of the other remarks that have been made I can see that we have the same kind of mentality on the part of some people that there was in this country in the 1870's when the railway to open up western Canada was being proposed. At that time there were many people who did not think it was of any very great importance and wanted to know what the taxpayers were going to get for their money. I think we should consider that this railway is not a railway to open up a mine or to open up any one particular community. It is a railroad to open up the northern part of this country in line with the policy that was outlined by the government,

a policy to which it committed itself and for the carrying out of which it received a mandate from the peeople of this country.
When we look at the matter from a purely dollars and cents point of view, certainly there is nobody in the house who would even be able to estimate what the returns to the country will be when the railroad has opened up that part of the country. We can see some of the benefits that will come about. We can appreciate that there will be an increase in the gross national product as soon as the mine at Pine Point is opened. I do not think there have been many projects started in Canada on such a basis as this one, namely a guarantee that the railroad is not going to lose any money with a private company having guaranteed in writing enough business to underwrite the cost of operation and maintenance of the railroad line. I do not think that the country has ever been in the position before of undertaking such an important development with all the costs being underwritten to this extent.
In addition to the increase in the gross national product that will result, there will, of course, be taxation thereon from which the federal treasury will benefit. I know it was estimated a number of years ago by the commissioner of the Northwest Territories, who presented a brief to the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects, that the business available then would result in an increase of $3J million in direct taxes payable to the federal treasury by the one mine that at that time contemplated starting operations. Since that time it has become quite apparent that there is going to be a good deal more business. When he made his estimate for the benefit of the royal commission the commissioner pointed out that was the direct financial return from one source and that all the other things involved would also result in the federal treasury receiving increased tax payments.
Then there are the benefits to the 77,000 people who live in the Peace River area. I am sure that the development of agriculture in that area will be of great benefit to this country and cannot be measured in dollars and cents. The bill represents the carrying out of a commitment that has been made by governments to the people in that area over the years, but this is the first government that has had the courage to make a decision and proceed with the opening up of the north. That is just what the government was elected by the people of this country to do.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few brief comments. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate commenced his argument by saying that he was making certain assumptions. Let me say that he has argued his assumptions very ably but his assumptions were all wrong.
The hon. member, as have other hon. members, proceeded on the assumption that this is a railway solely for the purpose of opening up a mine. I propose to refute that argument in specific detail.
In 1929 the Liberal party first raised the question of this railway to Great Slave lake. The Hon. Charles Dunning, then minister of railways, said: "I shall live to see this railway completed to Great Slave lake before I die." The Liberals placed in the statute relating to the Northern Alberta Railways a clause giving permission for this railway to be built.
If the railway had been built at the time it should have been built it would have cost far less than it will now cost. The hon. member for Laurier mentioned the figure of $50 million. I venture to suggest that if the railway had been built right after the war as it should have been it would probably have cost less than $40 million. If it had been built then there might well now be half a million people in that part of the country. The Northwest Territories could have developed to a stage that would have caused a tremendous expansion in our gross national product. There lies the fault of the previous administration. I am sorry that hon. members of the opposition have shut their ears and have refused to listen to the pearls of parliamentary wisdom which the minister has cast before them. I have some regard for the Liberal party, but the speech that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has just made will go far to cause the few remaining members of his party now crouching in fox holes in the northern part of this country to burrow even deeper.
I was in Yellowknife a short time ago. For the last few years that part of the country has been pausing in its development. It has been standing still simply because there is a stage in the opening up of an area when the cost of the necessary goods, commodities and services laid down becomes too great to justify development. This is something that the hon. member and 90205-6-561
Canadian National Railways his party might well have dealt with if they had done between 1948 and 1952 or 1953 what we are now doing.
I should like to deal very briefly with a remark made by the hon. member for Vancouver East. He cannot have been listening too well to his leader who has been criticizing the government for attempting to do bad things to the crown corporations. I was amazed to hear the hon. member advocate construction of this railway by the C.P.R. rather than the C.N.R. There is a reason for construction by the C.N.R. When Northern Alberta Railways was created in 1929 the people of the north country were bitterly opposed to it. They requested and petitioned that this 1,000-mile railway stretching into the northern regions of British Columbia and Alberta should be operated by Canadian National Railways because they knew that a period of development would be required which might well be attended to and looked after much better by the national railway company with respect to which the government might be able to exert some measure of persuasion.
In my opinion the people of the northern part of Canada are much happier that this new railway is going to be built by the C.N.R. I think this is their desire. I have been in touch with them and I know what they are thinking and saying. This decision will meet with their approval. There is a division of freight haulage between the two railway companies with which the minister dealt. For approximately two thirds of the distance over which the ore from Pine Point will be carried to its destination it will be transported on the railway lines of the national system while for the remaining one-third transportation will be over C.P.R. lines.
The hon. member for Vancouver East suggested the construction of a smelter. I spoke about that the other day. I should like to seee a smelter built at this time but in my opinion the economics of the situation do not justify that now. The situation in Trail at this time is that the economic operation of the smelter can only be carried on provided some 200,000 to 250,000 tons of lead and zinc concentrates are made available within the next two or three years. If that is not done, the operation will not continue to be economic. People will be laid off and it will be necessary for the company to go outside of Canada and purchase custom concentrates in order to maintain operations at a high economic level. That is not a major reason, of course, but it is a reason which the house must take into consideration, the maintenance of high employment so far as this operation is concerned.

Canadian National Railways
There is another point which I think hon. members of the opposition who have spoken have forgotten. I refer to the revenue that will accrue to the railway company not from this line itself, which we can call the incremental increase, but the revenue which will accrue to them on their main lines. A substantial amount of money will accrue to Canadian National Railways from the ore it will carry from Grimshaw to Calgary. Substantial revenue will also accrue to Canadian National Railways from the supplies it will transport to Pine Point. Substantial revenue will accrue to Canadian National Railways from the large amount of lumber it will haul from the area north of Grimshaw to eastern Canada.
Hon. members of the opposition have suggested there is no basis on which the government could have proceeded. The Manning royal commission sat for almost one year. There are several thousand pages in the transcript of the proceedings. They contain in great detail a full and ample account supported by the best witnesses who could be obtained and by briefs submitted by hardheaded business people from Vancouver, Edmonton, Montreal and the northern part of the country. The evidence all went to the root of the issue and indicated that in addition to the minerals which would be transported from Pine Point there would be other sources of revenue.
One of the commissioners, Mr. John Ander-son-Thomson, is a hard headed Scotsman who holds degrees as an engineer and as a surveyor. He has spent 25 to 30 years in the northern part of Canada and knows the country like the palm of his own hand. I had the privilege of appearing before the commission for almost five months and I heard the evidence submitted. The report is contained in a volume which is available to all hon. members and I am surprised that more of them have not read it. As found on page 83, Mr. Anderson-Thomson is dealing with agriculture and has this to say:
If half the potential arable land was developed together with more intensive cultivation of existing farms, tonnage to the railway would increase from 50,000 tons to 200,000 tons annually. This tonnage would include the incoming traffic. It would be reasonable to assume a subsidy on export grain to bring the rate up to 50 cents per 100 pounds giving a gross revenue to the C.P.R. and C.N.R. of $2 million per annum.
On page 86 of the report the same commissioner gives an estimate with regard to lumber. The estimate is based on statements made by the Alberta department of forestry which carries on a scientific inventory of the forest resources of this area. He indicates that if the total potential of the annual allowable cut is developed, and I do not anticipate that this will happen at once, of course,

there will be a total yearly revenue to the two railway companies of $3,600,000.
These are not the submissions of people who are biased. They are the findings of a responsible commissioner made after listening to the evidence brought before him and other members of the commission. They cannot be ignored. I know that the government has had reference to the evidence which was presented. I might say that a brief was presented to the commission by the commissioner of the Northwest Territories and a brief was also presented by Northern Alberta Railways on behalf of both the railway companies. These people knew what was involved. As a result of all these briefs and representations, here are the findings. I suggest that hon. members of the opposition take the time to read this report because in it they will find answers to all their questions.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to make only a few brief remarks on this matter. However, I was amazed to hear the hon. member for Westmorland say that the Liberals had always been opposed to the expansion of the Canadian National. All hon. members know I am not a supporter of the Liberal party. However, I have been in this house long enough to have heard on innumerable occasions when the Conservatives were in opposition and also when the Conservatives were in office, the Conservatives being the great supporters of the Canadian Pacific Railway. I feel that for any hon. member to say that the Liberals have been opposed to the expansion of the Canadian National is misrepresenting history in every sense.
Now, this particular extension of the Canadian National has the support of this group, Mr. Chairman. I do not want to cause any doubt about that; we support the bill now before us. However, we support it basically because there are tens of thousands of people living in the area that is going to be served by this extension of the railway, a number of whom have been living there for 40, 50 or 60 years. They moved into this territory on the distinct understanding that railway was going to be built to serve their needs. It is for this reason we support the bill now before us. We do not support it because of the needs of the mining industries located in the southern part of British Columbia and owned by the Canadian Pacific. We support it because of the farmers and the owners of lumbering industries in the region involved who are going to derive great benefit as a result of this extension of the railroad into northern Canada.
We are very suspicious, however, as to the reason the government has decided, at this particular time, to build this extension of the

Canadian railway system, from Grimshaw to Pine Point. We would immediately agree that a railway line ought to be built from Grimshaw to Fort Vermilion, but we fail to understand why it has to be built all the way up to Pine Point. If it is going to be a profitable undertaking, then I feel the Canadian Pacific would have decided to build this railroad. However, because the undertaking is of doubtful value, the taxpayers of Canada are being asked to build it.
I agree that the taxpayers of Canada ought to build it in so far as it is going to serve the settlers and the industries along the way. However, I do not for one moment believe that the taxpayers ought to be asked to subsidize the mining industries located down in Trail, British Columbia. There is no guarantee that this railway is going to operate at a profit. I have no particular quarrel with that aspect, if this railroad is going to meet our commitment to the settlers living in the Peace River area of Alberta. I believe it is up to the taxpayers to build a railroad to service the agricultural and lumbering interests in the area. However, if the extension up to Pine Point involves this railroad in a risk, then I feel that those who stand to benefit ought to run the risk, and that the Canadian Pacific ought to build this line.
We are going to support this bill. We are happy that the government has decided on the western route as opposed to the eastern. The construction of the eastern route might have pleased the people of Saskatchewan and of northeastern Alberta, but would have been much less satisfactory to the majority of the people who have an interest in this extension of our railways system. I say once again that in so far as this railroad extension is going to serve the interest of agriculture and lumbering we feel that in view of the promises that have been made over the past 40 or 50 years, the Canadian people owe it to these settlers to build this line. However, when it comes to building the line as far as Pine Point in order to deliver ores, we have severe reservations.
We feel that once again the government, this Conservative government, is being the willing stooge of the Canadian Pacific Railway. It is using the taxpayers' money in the hope of cashing in on the good will of the farmers and the lumbering interests. Over the years we have heard our Prime Minister, when he was in opposition, plead the cause of the Canadian Pacific until his heart really bled. We have seen the decisions rendered in relation to T.C.A. and C.P.A., and we have seen innumerable other respects in which this government has been a staunch defender of the Canadian Pacific. Once again, we have reason to suspect that it is not really the 90205-6-561i
Canadian National Railways lumbermen of northwestern Alberta, it is not really the farmers of northwestern Alberta, about whom this government is concerned, but it is the interests of the Canadian Pacific Railway. Even the Canadian Pacific seems to be in doubt about the economics of transporting ores from Great Slave lake down to Trail because that railway is unwilling to run the risk involved in constructing the line. The taxpayers of Canada, therefore, are being asked to be the goats.
Nevertheless, Mr. Chairman, in the interests of the farmers and those engaged in lumbering in northwestern Alberta, we are going to be very happy to support this bill with the reservation that we feel once more this government has bled its heart out for the welfare of the Canadian Pacific as opposed to the public interests.

In order to establish transportation services to and from mining properties in the area of Great Slave lake, in the Northwest Territories, and otherwise to assist in the development of northern Canada, the governor in council may provide for the construction-
I emphasize that line, "and otherwise to assist in the development of northern Canada".
Again in the draft agreement which has been presented to the committee and in the preamble speaking about the development of the railway they say: for the purpose of providing railway service for the development of the northern region of Canada. Again, to emphasize and reiterate, as it appears that is the only way in which to get the point over to members of the opposition, I should like to refer to the minister's statement as found at page 8504 of Hansard of September 18. In summing up the advantages of this particular railway he said this:
In other words, the proposed railway would be somewhat different from most branch lines constructed in recent years which were designed to service one mine or a group of mines. Its purpose, in fact, is to open up a whole new region.
The Great Slave lake railway will therefore be for the general development of the north.
The reason I wish to draw this matter to the attention of the committee is the fact that, coming as I do from British Columbia, I can say that we also share in the Peace River

Canadian National Railways block a block that has a population of some 70,000 people. We are also very fortunate in having the Pacific Great Eastern railway which connects Vancouver with the Peace River area up to Fort St. John. I think that it is the first stage of the development of further expansion of the north by converting by present methods a vision into a reality. I feel that members of the opposition have ignored the fact that it is approximately 40 miles or 50 miles from Fort St. John to Grimshaw, or in other words, the connecting up of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway with the Great Slave lake railway.
I bring this matter to the attention of the committee for this reason. If we take the average cost, which is approximately $171,000 per mile of development, I think that at a cost of well under $1 million, this connection could be made with the Pacific Great Eastern railway which taps the lower Vancouver area or the lower Vancouver mainland, an area with a population of approximately 1 million. I think the Pacific Great Eastern itself has shown its success as I believe the completion of the P.G.E. developed the lumber business to a point where it was ten times what it had been before the P.G.E. was completed to the north.
I mention this matter because it has not been drawn to the attention of the committee. We have had briefs during the course of this year and submissions from the province of British Columbia, the British Columbia and Yukon chamber of mines, the city of Dawson Creek, the north Vancouver board of trade and the Vancouver board of trade. They have shown their tangible interest in the development of that great area. 1 think this is one of the factors that must be considered for by developing this railway to the north and eventually looking towards the future expansion of the P.G.E., we are also helping the development of British Columbia as well as Alberta. I feel that members of the committee should support this extremely important bill, taking the long range viewpoint.

In speaking briefly to Bill No. C-126, I would point out the difficulty of some of us sitting on this side of the chamber in that we do not have confidence in the economic judgment of this government; nor do we have any reason to believe that this project, in the form in which it is presented to the committee tonight, is the result of any economic analysis or contract in any way having in mind the general interest of Canada.
In reply to interrogation the minister has answered that certain inquiries and investigations were made by governmental experts. If he made that statement, I know that would be so. On the other hand, we are mindful of the fact that when the present leader of the government was in opposition and campaigning he made precisely these pronouncements, namely that this project was economic, that all this was desirable, that this was his vision and that this would be one of the things he would do if he presided over the government of Canada. I refer to the Montreal Star of April 26, 1957:
With a declaration that "this is a time for planning for greatness in Canada's future" Mr. Diefenbaker urged that the national policy of Sir John A. Macdonald for developing the West be adapted to changing times and applied to the northland.
"The North with its vast stores of hidden wealth is ready to come into its own" he said. "The wonder and challenge of the North must become our national consciousness. All that is needed is an imaginative policy which will open its doors to Canadian initiative and enterprise.
Almost in the same terms he expressed himself in his opening campaign address

delivered in Massey Hall in Toronto on April 25, 1957, with the same slogan "The New Frontier Policy". This was a policy declared far and wide before it was analysed. It was a slogan before there was any economic or indeed geological study to substantiate or support it.
I take very strong issue with the conclusions from some of the suggested economic studies which have been later put forward by other members of this committee. I put it to you, Mr. Chairman, that in other economic prognostications the right hon. gentleman now holding the position of Prime Minister has been quite wrong; and that the Minister of Finance in the budget address of March 21, 1957, one of the rudest budget addresses in the history of our parliament gave a firm commitment for a balanced budget. We in the course of these last years know how completely imbalanced his own budgets have become.
We recognize the fact that the entire Northwest Territories, whose southerly boundary is approximately 50 miles north of Skagway, Alaska, have a population approximately the same as that of my small home town of Brockville, namely something under 20,000 people. I refer to my own small town paper the Recorder and Times which has an article headed "Relief Payments Here Hit Record High Level". I will not read the article in detail. It is to be found in the issue of September 22, 1961.
We all believe in development but we believe also in proportion. If this government is able to present a bill which presents possibilities for future development which are perhaps not entirely economic but which offer some prospects for people on the frontier well and good. Incidentally, I may say that we may not have these people for long because as the hon. lady presiding over the Department of Citizenship and Immigration knows, the present picture seems to indicate that our population is moving out of Canada. I put it to the committee that even if this were not entirely economical we might be quite interested-

There has been a reversal. At this particular moment in history we come to the situation where we must examine an interesting part of the frontier, with perhaps tremendous possibilities in the future, and with 20,000 people there now. We are asked to put $86 million into this project, or perhaps it will be $125 million, because we have not had any firm estimate in support of the cost. We have no idea what the cost of this railway will be to Canada.
Also, when we examine this agreement, which we have only had an opportunity to examine within the last few hours, we find 17 pages of extremely complicated drafting, with a great deal of mathematics in it. I have been unable to discover where there is any benefit to the chief contracting party, Her Majesty the Queen in right of Canada. The preamble says:
Whereas the government desires the construction of a line of railway from a point at or near Grimshaw, Alberta, on the Northern Alberta Railway's line, to Great Slave lake,-
That is almost in the language of the present Prime Minister as he started his campaign at Massey Hall in 1957. But we see nothing else in the 17 foolscap pages of this document to suggest that Her Majesty the Queen gets a penny out of this project now or in the future. All we hear about is more dream or vision, and we have serious unemployment to cope with in the populous parts of Ontario and Quebec and in the east and in the west. This sounds to me somewhat out of proportion.
Again, when we look at this agreement we find four contracting parties. As other hon, members have mentioned, we have a situation where Her Majesty gets nothing now and nothing in the future, at a time of enormous public deficit, perhaps the largest deficit we will have in Canada's history.
The contracting party, Canadian National Railway Company, will probably not lose very

Canadian National Railways much. It cannot, surely, gain anything substantial except at our cost. Pine Point Mines Limited is 78 per cent owned by Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company which is 50 per cent owned by C.P.R. which is 30 per cent owned by the Canadian people.
Who is getting this great big give-away? This is one of the things we have to be concerned about. If we look back just a few decades in history we will recall that one of the worries about the development of the west was the extent to which Conservative governments were developing this kind of project by a process of give-away. We believe in development. We think there has to be a development of the northlands. But there has to be a bit of quid pro quo in this matter. If there is not any clear benefit coming to Canadian people, I think frankly we have a duty to stand up at this time and say so.
